title: Corrupt PNG image in request returns HTTP 500 "broken PNG file (chunk ...)" instead of a client error
body: A chat completion request containing a **structurally-corrupted PNG** (garbage chunk header after a truncated IDAT stream) returns **HTTP 500** with the raw Pillow exception message, instead of a client-side 400 error. Sending invalid image data is a client problem, so it should fail fast with a clear 400 like other malformed images do. Minimal reproduction — serve any vision-language model (reproduced with `google/gemma-4-26b-A4B-it` on the nightly above; the failure is in the model-agnostic media loading path) and send: Actual response (HTTP 500): Expected: HTTP 400 with a message like `Failed to load image: broken PNG file (chunk ...)`, consistent with the other malformed-image paths. For comparison, the **same server** already returns a proper 400 for other corrupt input: - random non-image bytes → `400 BadRequestError: Failed to load image: cannot identify image file <_io.BytesIO object>` - truncated PNG → `400` (OSError path) Only the chunk-structure corruption takes the 500 path. `ImageMediaIO.load_bytes` (`vllm/multimodal/media/image.py`) wraps decode failures in a client-facing `ValueError`, but its except clause only catches `(OSError, Image.UnidentifiedImageError)`. Pillow raises a plain **`SyntaxError`** ("broken PNG file") for corrupted chunk structures — which is neither — so it escapes unwrapped, and the request-level error mapper only promotes `ValueError` to `BadRequestError` (unmapped exceptions become `InternalServerError`).
label: bug

title: EXIF-oriented images (orientation != 1) return 500 on mistral-tokenizer models: "Expected there to be 1 prompt placeholders ... found 0"
body: Sending a JPEG whose EXIF orientation tag is not 1 (e.g. any Samsung phone photo, orientation 6) to a VLM served with `--tokenizer-mode mistral` fails with HTTP 500: - Orientation 1 images work. - Orientation 6/8 (90°/270°) always fail with the error above. - Orientation 3 (180°) does **not** fail, but the model receives pixels in a different layout than mistral_common's own decode (silent inconsistency: the model answers orientation questions as if the image was pre-rotated, while the `[IMG]` token grid was computed from the un-rotated decode). **Root cause** (identified while debugging): with `--tokenizer-mode mistral`, the prompt is rendered by mistral_common's chat template, which decodes the image from the original bytes **without** applying the EXIF transpose. vLLM's `ImageMediaIO.load_bytes` applies it (`normalize_image`, introduced in #44974). For orientations that swap width/height (6/8), the image token grid computed from the two decodes disagrees, so placeholder validation finds 0 `[IMG]` placeholders for 1 image item. The two decodes must agree. 1. Serve any mistral-format VLM, e.g.: 2. Send a chat completion containing an EXIF-6 JPEG (any Samsung portrait photo) via `POST /v1/chat/completions` with an `image_url` data-URI. 3. Observed: HTTP 500 with the placeholder error. The same image re-encoded with orientation stripped returns 200. Minimal generator for the four common orientations (identical pixels, only the tag differs — `pip install pillow`): Note: the image must be **non-square** — a square image produces the same token grid with or without the transpose and does not trigger the 500. EXIF-oriented images are served normally (HTTP 200), with vLLM's decode matching the mistral_common chat-template decode — the same behavior as the reference mistral_common inference stack.
label: bug

title: Cold-cache KV cache OOM with `--kv-cache-memory-bytes` and `--enable-sleep-mode`
body: RTX 5090 32 GB (SM120), driver 617.14, Windows 11 + WSL2 (Ubuntu 26.04), torch 2.13.0+cu130, FlashInfer 0.7.0.post1, vLLM nightly `0.32.0rc1.dev35+g656d0d450`. **Problem.** With `--kv-cache-memory-bytes` and `--enable-sleep-mode`, a start with empty compile caches (first start after install or upgrade) of the command below fails while allocating the KV cache (`allocate_kv_cache`, `vllm/v1/worker/utils.py`): With warm caches the same command started in our tests, so the failure looks intermittent. Seen with both `--kv-cache-dtype fp8` and `nvfp4`. The model's weights are NVFP4, which is where the buffer below comes from; other weight formats were not tested, but the missing guards are not format-specific. v0.31.0 also lacks both in this branch (not run). **Cause.** The `kv_cache_memory_bytes` branch of `Worker.determine_available_memory()` runs `profile_run()` without either allocator guard that the memory-profiling branch has: 1. **No cache release.** `memory_profiling` runs `gc.collect()` and `empty_cache()` on exit; this branch does not, so fully free cached segments (2.4 GiB here) stay reserved. The open PR #59893 adds this release. 2. **No split limit.** #58430 runs the memory-profiling `profile_run()` inside `_scoped_allocator_max_split(max_split_size_mb=20)`; this branch does not. A snapshot just before KV allocation (both instrumented unpatched cold starts) showed a 2,426 MiB segment kept reserved by a single live 40 MiB FlashInfer scratch buffer (`flashinfer/utils.py` `_get_cache_buf`, from `mm_fp4`). `empty_cache()` cannot release that segment while the scratch buffer remains live; with #59893 alone, device-free memory also stayed lower after start-up and after a 10,408-token request. With sleep mode the KV cache is allocated in the separate CuMem pool, so these retained default-pool reservations reduce the device memory available to it. `VLLM_ENABLE_STARTUP_PLAN=1` also sets `kv_cache_memory_bytes` (from a saved plan), so those starts take the same branch.
label: bug

title: Tool-call argument coercion turns string values such as "0017" into integers for ["string", "integer"] parameters
body: For a tool parameter whose schema admits both `string` and `integer` (`"type": ["string", "integer"]`, or the equivalent `anyOf`), the Qwen3 engine tool parser (`qwen3_coder`, `qwen3_xml`, `mimo`) coerces the raw parameter text with `vllm.tool_parsers.utils.coerce_to_schema_type`. That function tries `integer` before `string` and returns `int(value)` whenever `int()` succeeds. A string value that only looks like an integer therefore reaches the client as a different integer: - `0017` becomes `17` (leading zeros lost), - `1_000` becomes `1000`, - `+17` becomes `17`. Quoting the value does not help: `"0017"` is kept as a string that includes the quote characters (`"\"0017\""`). For such a parameter, no model output can deliver the string `"0017"` to the client. We hit this in practice with Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B served through the OpenAI-compatible server. The user message asked the model to pass the **string** `'0017'`; the model wrote `<parameter=value>\n0017\n</parameter>`, and the client received `{"value": 17}`. Re-sampling the same request through `/v1/completions` (no tool parser) showed the model writing `0017` in every sample. Leading zeros and similar forms matter for identifiers, ZIP codes, account numbers and version components, and the change is silent to the application. Minimal reproduction (only the tokenizer is downloaded; no GPU or model weights needed): Output with vLLM 0.31.0: The same code path is present on `main` (da9134bc89364465f68aa679564435936d157a14): `coerce_to_schema_type` in `vllm/tool_parsers/utils.py` still returns `int(value)` for the `integer` candidate before considering `string`. **Expected behavior.** When `string` is an admissible type, coercion should preserve what the model wrote. One option is to accept a numeric coercion only when it round-trips to the original text, e.g. `str(int(value)) == value` for `integer` (and the analogous check for `number`), and otherwise fall back to the next type, which is `string`. `0017`, `1_000` and `

title: speculative_config.method="ngram_gpu" with compilation_config.mode="NONE" kills engine init — ValueError: No compilation mode is set.
body: `speculative_config.method="ngram_gpu"` (the GPU n-gram speculative-decoding proposer) constructs its kernel unconditionally through `TorchCompileWithNoGuardsWrapper`, so it **depends** on `compilation_config` actually having a compile backend. There is no compatibility check between `compilation_config.mode` and `speculative_config.method`: when the user explicitly disables compilation (`mode="NONE"` — a documented value, whose purpose is to skip the torch.compile overhead), the engine raises while constructing the drafter inside `GPUModelRunnerV1.__init__`. Two problems: 1. **The error does not point at the parameter the user set.** `ValueError: No compilation mode is set.` says neither that `compilation_config.mode="NONE"` caused it, nor that `ngram_gpu` needs a compile backend. A user reading that line will go and re-check their `compilation_config` spelling, even though "disable compilation" is perfectly valid for ordinary models (in the same batch, `mode="NONE"` + `method="ngram"` points all started and generated normally). 2. **The validation happens far too late.** Both values are individually legal, and the conflict only surfaces in EngineCore's `init_device`. It could be decided in `create_engine_config()` with a message naming both sides of the conflict and the way out. Control (same model, same `compilation_config`, only the proposer switched to the CPU-trie `ngram`): the engine starts and generates normally. Either reject the combination cleanly at `create_engine_config()` time, naming both sides of the conflict and the way out: or make `ngram_gpu` fall back to a proposer that does not need compilation, instead of being constructed and then failing. title: /pause clears SHM multimodal cache, can cause fatal ValueError for queued requests
body: With `--mm-processor-cache-type shm`, `POST /pause?mode=keep` (or `mode=wait` with `clear_cache=true`), while image requests are waiting to be scheduled, can kill the engine as soon as one of them is scheduled, see log: Every in-flight and later request then fails, and `/health` stops answering 200. `/pause?mode=keep` is documented to ignore `clear_cache` ("Ignored when mode=keep"), so tecnically a keep pause is not expected to touch any cache at all. title: Stop sequences match inside reasoning, so responses come back empty (breaks Claude Code auto mode)
body: vLLM `main` @ `ae8f41238c`, 8xH100, served with `just serve` equivalent: Stop sequences are checked against the model's reasoning, not just the answer. If the reasoning contains the stop string, generation ends inside `<think>` and the response has **no text**. This breaks Claude Code's auto mode on vLLM. Its safety classifier sends `stop_sequences: ["</block>"]` and expects `<block>yes|no`. The model often writes `<block>no</block>` while thinking, so the request stops before the answer and the classifier gets no verdict. Claude Code then retries the check or escalates to its slower second stage, which adds latency and extra calls (see the comment below for traces across Claude Code versions). Without `stop_sequences`, the response is correct: The same request with `"stop_sequences": ["</block>"]` comes back empty (the end of the thinking block is shown for clarity): It reproduces in **100/100** requests. `/v1/chat/completions` with `"stop": ["</block>"]` behaves the same way: `content: null`, and the reasoning is cut off at `<block>no`. Stop sequences should only apply to the answer, after `</think>`. The model would then finish reasoning and return `<block>no`. That is how hosted APIs behave. - #53066 (same root cause, found via lm-eval) - #58647 item 3 (Claude Code `/v1/messages` hardening RFC) - Open fixes: #52486, #38533 AI assistance (Claude Code) was used to investigate and write this issue.
label: bug

title: `vllm serve --uds <path>` cannot be restarted on the same path: the socket file is never removed, so the second start fails with `[Errno 98] Address already in use`
body: A Unix-domain socket file outlives the process that bound it. vLLM never removes it: `create_server_unix_socket` (`vllm/entrypoints/launchers/launcher.py`) only does `sock.bind(path)`, and every shutdown path (`run_server_worker`, `run_multi_api_server`, the render and snapshot servers) only calls `sock.close()`. So after a clean `SIGTERM`, `vllm serve --uds /run/vllm.sock` leaves `/run/vllm.sock` on disk, and starting the server again on the same path fails during startup: This is a stale-file error, not a running server: nothing accepts connections on the path (`connect()` returns `ECONNREFUSED`). Every restart of a `--uds` deployment (systemd unit, container with a mounted socket directory, supervisor) therefore needs an external `rm` of the socket file first. uvicorn's own `--uds` mode does not have this problem, because asyncio's `create_unix_server(path=...)` removes a leftover socket file before binding; vLLM bypasses that by handing uvicorn a pre-bound socket. Mechanism, no model needed: End to end (1x A100-40GB, `Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B`): Measured (1x A100-40GB, `Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B --enforce-eager`, vLLM 0.31.0): first start healthy after ~110 s and served a completion over the socket; `SIGTERM` → clean exit, socket file still present; second start on the same path exited with the error above. With the proposed fix applied to the same 0.31.0 tree: socket file removed on shutdown, second start healthy after ~55 s, `GET /health` → 200. The second start succeeds, as it does with a TCP port: a leftover socket file that nothing listens on is removed before binding, and the server removes its own socket file on shutdown. A path that another live server still listens on should still be refused. In `create_server_unix_socket`, probe an existing socket file with `connect()`; on `ECONNREFUSED` remove it before `bind()` (a live listener is left alone, a regular file is not touched). The Triton compiler rejects an FP8 `tl.dot` with K = 16. `--kv-cache-dtype auto` works. SM89 is expected to fail the same way, since the Triton rule does not depend on the architecture, but I did not run it. From the source, the affected code is in v0.32.0rc0 and later; it is not in v0.31.x. Reproduction (dummy weights, reduced to 4 layers; layers 0 and 3 keep the real full-attention shape, 64 query / 4 KV heads): - The reduced model still loads 21.6 GiB of weights, so this repro needs a GPU with more than 24 GB. - Dummy weights and the layer reduction do not matter here: the error is a compile-time shape/dtype check. **With MTP**, the engine fails at startup: Full server logs of all runs (with and without MTP, chunked prefill): https://gist.github.com/yuy-blip/9984f7a03950ea5e84f150ae63b60881 **Without `--speculative-config`**, the server starts and the first request kills the engine with the same `K >= 32` error: That prompt is 5 tokens. A long prompt can fail too, when chunked prefill leaves a short last chunk. With `--max-num-batched-tokens 256 --no-enable-prefix-caching`: - prompts of 256 + 2, 256 + 5 and 256 + 8 tokens kill the engine; - 256 + 9 and 256 + 20 tokens are served. Expected: the server starts and serves, as it does with `--kv-cache-dtype auto`. Cause, as far as I can tell: - FP8 KV cache is a supported configuration for this backend since #58128 (`fp8` / `fp8_e4m3` are in `TritonAttentionDiffKVBackend.supported_kv_cache_dtypes`).
label: bug

title: ORCA endpoint-load-metrics reports only one engine's load under data parallel
body: `collect_env.py` fails on macOS with the `AssertionError` from #57671, so I ran it with `get_pkg_version` stubbed to return `None`, which only affects the Intel XPU package fields `get_named_metrics_from_prometheus()` in `vllm/entrypoints/serve/utils/orca_metrics.py` reads `vllm:kv_cache_usage_perc` and `vllm:num_requests_waiting`, which have one sample per engine. When one API server fronts several engines (data parallel with internal LB), it appends every sample without aggregating them. JSON keeps only the last engine's values. TEXT repeats each key once per engine, so a parser that keeps the last value sees the same thing. Gateways use the `endpoint-load-metrics` header for load-aware routing. A server with engine 0 at 95% KV usage and 40 waiting requests and engine 1 at 5% KV usage and 0 waiting reports only engine 1's values (5% and 0). This can lead a load-aware gateway to prefer it over servers that are less loaded. This also happens without skew, as two engines with 20 waiting requests each report 20 instead of 40. Repro (CPU only, no server): Observed: Expected with the fix below: Proposed fix: - Sum `num_requests_waiting` across engines. - Average `kv_cache_usage_perc` across engines. This is the fraction of the endpoint's KV cache in use, assuming engines of equal size. - Pass `metrics_format` instead of the builtin `format` to the unsupported-format warning. It currently logs `` `<built-in function format>` format is not supported in the ORCA response header``. - Lower the `Created ORCA header` log from info to debug. It fires on every response that includes the header.
label: bug

title: Shutdown stalls ~90s: every TP rank unpins the full shared host pool and EngineCore blocks on dying workers
body: Shutting down a HiSparse server (TP8, `--shutdown-timeout 90`) stalls for about 90s. The API server eventually force-kills EngineCore. The cause is the HiSparse pinned host pool: every worker has to unpin it, and EngineCore can't exit until all workers have done so. Requests drain immediately. All of the time is spent waiting for the worker processes to die. 1. **Every TP rank pins the entire shared host region.** `allocate_hisparse_host_pools` (`vllm/v1/hisparse/runtime.py`) calls `cudaHostRegister` on the whole shared `/dev/shm` mmap in every rank. Each rank must therefore unpin all of it on exit, and the ranks contend with each other while doing so. 2. **The 5s worker grace period is far too short.** `VLLM_WORKER_SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT_SECONDS=5` expires long before `release_pinned_state()` finishes, so shutdown always falls through to SIGTERM and then SIGKILL. The `HiSparse: unpinned X GiB ...` log line never appears. 3. **SIGKILL doesn't help.** The kernel still has to unpin every page during process exit, and this is *slower* than a graceful `cudaHostUnregister`. 4. **EngineCore blocks on the dying workers with no timeout.** `_ensure_worker_termination` returns right after `p.kill()`. The workers are `daemon=True`, so Python's multiprocessing atexit handler (`_exit_function`) joins them with no timeout. EngineCore can't exit until the kernel finishes tearing them down, which ends in the API server's force-kill. The stall is invisible because the EngineCore teardown logs are debug-level. The script below copies HiSparse's shared-pool setup: N spawned daemon processes each `mmap` one `/dev/shm` file and `cudaHostRegister` all of it. It then times either graceful unregister or SIGKILL. I ran it on H100s with 7 processes on 7 GPUs: | Pool | register (per proc) | graceful unregister (per proc) | all procs gone after SIGKILL | |---|---|---|---| | 16 GiB | 3.6–4.3s | 0.4–1.1s | 3.6s | | 64 GiB | 17s | – | ~20s | | 128 GiB | ~30.5s | 2.9 → 13.5s (one after another) | 21.7s
label: bug

title: quantization="mxfp4" on CUDA reports "No MXFP4 MoE backend supports the deployment configuration" while listing only AMD backends (AITER / amd-quark)
body: On a **CUDA** device, `quantization="mxfp4"` passes `EngineArgs.create_engine_config()` and then fails during MoE backend selection with a message that (a) blames the *deployment configuration* and (b) enumerates **only AMD/ROCm backends** as candidates: Why this is worth fixing: 1. **Cross-vendor diagnosis leak.** Both candidates are AMD-only (AITER is a ROCm library; `amd-quark` is an AMD quantization package). On a CUDA machine the user is told to set `VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1` / install `amd-quark`, neither of which can ever help. Nothing says "this platform has no MXFP4 MoE kernel". 2. **The message misattributes the cause.** "No MXFP4 MoE backend supports the *deployment configuration*" implies the user's configuration is at fault, when in fact the candidate set on CUDA is empty by construction. A user with a perfectly ordinary config is sent debugging their own settings. 3. **No actionable next step.** The message does not say whether MXFP4 is expected to work on CUDA at all in this build, nor which alternative quantization to use instead. A message that names the real situation and a usable fallback, e.g.: Ideally the platform check happens at config-validation time, so the engine is never built for a configuration that cannot be served. title: enable_lora on Jamba (ai21labs/Jamba-tiny-dev) causes a CUDA illegal memory access followed by an uncaught C++ exception (`terminate called ... c10::AcceleratorError`) during startup
body: Enabling LoRA on `ai21labs/Jamba-tiny-dev` makes the EngineCore process hit a CUDA illegal memory access during startup, and because the error escapes as an uncaught C++ exception the process aborts instead of failing gracefully: Two things make this more serious than the other LoRA precondition gaps: 1. **It is not a clean rejection.** An illegal address fault can corrupt the CUDA context; a `terminate` means no orderly teardown and no usable error contract for the caller. 2. **It is reproducible with a rank well inside the documented limit** (`max_lora_rank=32`), so it is not the known `max_lora_rank<=128` kernel-capacity assertion. The reporting site is untrustworthy by construction — the first traceback in the log ends in `vllm/ir/ops/layernorm.py` `rms_norm`, but CUDA errors are reported asynchronously, so the faulting kernel may precede it. The stack should be re-taken with `CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1`. To localize the faulting kernel: Either LoRA starts successfully on Jamba, or the unsupported combination is rejected at config time. In no case should a user-settable flag combination produce a CUDA illegal memory access and a hard process abort. Config accepted → EngineCore init → model build / profiling forward → `torch.AcceleratorError: CUDA error: an illegal memory access was encountered` → exception escapes through the C++ layer → `terminate called after throwing an instance of 'c10::AcceleratorError'` → EngineCore aborts → client sees `RuntimeError: Engine core initialization failed`. - vLLM: 0.31.0 (official wheel) - PyTorch: 2.13.0+cu130, CUDA 13.0, driver 580.82.07 - GPU: NVIDIA RTX 5880 Ada Generation (sm89), 47.4 GiB (verified free at run time: ~49 GB) - OS: Ubuntu 22.04.4 LTS (glibc 2.35), Python 3.12.13 - Model: `ai21labs/Jamba-tiny-dev` - Found by a config-interaction test generator (point used `enable_cumem_allocator`, `enable_lora`, `max_lora_rank=32`, `specialize_active_lora`, `use_fp64_gumbel`), then isolated standalone to `enable_lora` + `max_lo

title: Olmo-Hybrid-7B fails to load with default settings — GDN fused conv1d weight loader indexes `dims[loaded_shard_id]` while `loaded_shard_id` defaults to `None`
body: `allenai/Olmo-Hybrid-7B` cannot be loaded with default settings. During weight loading, the GDN layer's fused conv1d weight loader unconditionally indexes a per-section dimension list with `loaded_shard_id`, but that parameter's default value is `None`: The loader is registered with `set_weight_loader`/auto-loading, which invokes it **without** `loaded_shard_id`, so it raises immediately: The user-visible symptom is only `RuntimeError: Engine core initialization failed`; the real cause is buried in EngineCore stderr. title: DSpark draft token count inflated by reusing target DP sync state with adaptive verification
body: With adaptive verification and DP enabled, DSpark reuses the target model’s DP sync state, whose `num_reqs` may reflect the target CUDA graph’s padded request capacity rather than the logical request count. title: fused_recurrent KDA path loads the per-key gate g without a mask, resulting in out-of-bounds reads
body: In `fused_recurrent_gated_delta_rule_fwd_kernel`, the KDA branch loads the per-key gate with no mask, while every other per-timestep load uses `mask_k` / `mask_v`: When `K` is not a power of two (`K=100`, so `BK=128`), lanes `K..BK-1` read past the end of each row. title: Harden logit_bias against absolute-logit leakage
body: Following private triage with the vLLM security team, I am opening this as a hardening request, as they suggested. Adding a user-provided bias directly to FP32 logits can make the greedy winner depend on a common offset of the input scores. This can happen even when all relative logits remain unchanged. Under the tested conditions, repeated bias queries can recover absolute pre-bias logits from token IDs alone. The practical impact demonstrated so far is limited. I would like to discuss centering the FP32 logits before finite, nonzero bias addition, by subtracting the maximum score. Centering after the addition is too late to remove the rounding difference. The main points to decide are where to apply this in the sampling pipeline and whether it should be enabled by default. Centering preserves softmax probabilities in exact arithmetic, but it can change near-tie decisions and later repetition penalties. It also adds a reduction over the vocabulary, so serving overhead needs measurement. - An operator-controlled option could preserve the existing default behavior. - Operators could reject `logit_bias` requests, but this also removes useful token steering. - Centering only after bias addition does not fix the example below. **Small numerical example.** This uses only Python's standard library to show the FP32 rounding effect; it is not an end-to-end vLLM recovery script. Token IDs are 0 and 1, with the first index winning ties. **Relevant vLLM 0.31.0 code:** [FP32 conversion and processor order](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/v0.31.0/vllm/v1/worker/gpu/sample/sampler.py) and [the bias addition kernel](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/v0.31.0/vllm/v1/worker/gpu/sample/logit_bias.py). The tested V2 runner applies bias after copying logits to FP32. A regression should compare bias-query outputs across stored FP32 vectors related by an exact common shift. An implementation should also cover empty/zero biases, token masks and all-masked rows, and evalu

Non-Harmony models already return logprobs on this endpoint via `_create_response_logprobs`, so gpt-oss users can't get token confidence scores for evals, scoring, or RL workflows through the Responses API. **Proposed approach** 1. Attach logprobs only to `final`-channel content tokens (excluding Harmony control tokens such as `<|channel|>`, `<|message|>`, `<|end|>`), reusing `_create_response_logprobs`. 3. title: TTL-based Eviction for KV Cache Blocks
body: As you may know, major LLM providers apply a retention period to stored KV cache. For example, OpenAI retains the KV cache for GPT-5.6 and later models for 30 minutes after its most recent read or write ([source](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching#cache-lifetime-gpt-5-6-and-later)). vLLM has only limited support for this. The only relevant option I could find is `decoder_kv_blocks_ttl` ([source](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/design/nixl_kv_cache_lease/#bidirectional-kv-transfer)), which sets time-based eviction for KV cache stored on the GPUs of the decode stage in PD disaggregation. Beyond that, based on [this discussion](https://discuss.vllm.ai/t/how-to-adjust-prefix-caching-timeout/1663) and [this GitHub issue](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/8333), vLLM doesn’t support TTL-based prefix cache eviction. Note that what I have in mind is simpler than memory pinning, as discussed in GitHub issues #51428 and #37003. vLLM would keep its existing LRU eviction as is, but [`KVCacheBlock`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/624a5ddafd96df23fe2b9f6d4b8f52a08b9fe9ea/vllm/v1/core/kv_cache_utils.py#L154) would gain an `expires_at` field, and a block would be lazily evicted after expiration time is passed. So my question is: would this feature be useful for vLLM? I’ve already implemented the eviction method described above and would like to open a PR. Since a PR involves more than just sharing code, I wanted to check first whether there’s interest. title: Enable batch-sharded sampling for GPT-OSS
body: Batch-sharded sampling was introduced in #50465, but GPT-OSS does not implement the required `compute_logits_local` interface. With Model Runner V2, enabling `--enable-batch-sharded-sampling` therefore logs a warning and falls back to regular sampling. GPT-OSS uses the standard `ParallelLMHead` and `LogitsProcessor`, so it should be possible to enable the existing path by exposing rank-local logits with `skip_gather=True`. This would allow GPT-OSS to distribute sampling work across TP ranks. In development benchmarks with GPT-OSS-20B on 2×L20, TP=2, and concurrency 256, enabling this path improved output throughput by approximately 4.5–6.0%. Continue using regular sampling. This works correctly but does not benefit from batch-sharded sampling. The proposed change is limited to the model hook and regression coverage in the existing sharded-sampling E2E test. Logits redistribution and sampling remain handled by the shared runner. Related: #56074, which addresses compatibility with lm_head LoRA.

title: Allow pooling tasks (token_embed / token_classify) to reuse prefix cache while returning full hidden-state sequences
body: On vLLM 0.29.0, pooling requests with `task="token_embed"` or `task="token_classify"` are **forcefully excluded from prefix-cache reads**, even when prefix caching is explicitly enabled and the caller explicitly requests it. The mandatory behavior is in `vllm/pooling_params.py` (`_merge_default_parameters`, present in v0.29.0 through current `main`): When the caller leaves `skip_reading_prefix_cache` as `None` (the default), it is forced to `True` for these two tasks. There is no supported way for an application to opt in to cache reads while keeping the pooling task. Our workload is multi-candidate classification with a sequence-classification adapter (`vllm-jev`, serving Open-Jev-2B style decision heads). For each HTTP request: 1. The prompt is built as `fixed instructions + fixed candidate list (up to ~18 candidates) + per-request state`, so **the leading ~400+ tokens are identical across requests** and only the trailing state differs. 2. The adapter submits one pooling request per candidate (or a deduplicated set of shared-prefix sequences) with `task="token_embed"`, because the decision head needs **the hidden states at specific readout positions** of the full sequence — a scalar `classify` output is not sufficient. 3. Many candidates share the same leading tokens, and the fixed instruction/criteria block is repeated across every request. This is exactly the workload prefix caching is designed for. With the forced skip, every request recomputes the entire prompt. Measured on an RTX 4090 (vLLM 0.29.0, prefix caching enabled, same `cache_salt`, identical prompts re-submitted back-to-back): - `metadata.cached_tokens` is always `0` for both `token_embed` and `classify` pooling requests; - the engine-level `Prefix cache hit rate` metric does occasionally report small non-zero values (2.6%–5.1%), so the cache subsystem itself is alive — but per-request `num_cached_tokens` stays 0 and our throughput matches the "no reuse" expectation; - using `--decision-template` sty

title: Explicitly trust a selected preload daemon to avoid checkpoint rescans on engine restart
body: When an engine starts with `--load-format ipc_cache`, it computes the checkpoint fingerprint again before requesting weights from a preload daemon. On a high-latency filesystem, that scan can take a meaningful fraction of every engine restart even when the operator intends to reuse the same already-loaded daemon. I propose an explicit opt-in mode in which the operator selects a particular live preload daemon instance and declares its resident weights authoritative. In this mode, the engine would skip reading checkpoint files to recompute the content fingerprint. It should still check the model architecture, dtype, quantization configuration, parallel layout, vLLM version, and physical GPU compatibility against the selected daemon. This would be an operator-controlled invalidation contract: changing the source checkpoint would require starting a new preload daemon. The default behavior should continue to validate checkpoint content. The opt-in should be visible in startup logs, including the identity of the daemon being trusted and the requirement to re-preload after source changes. The identity and lifecycle semantics need design discussion. In particular, the engine must not silently trust a different daemon that later occupies the same socket path. A daemon instance identifier or generation, rather than only a socket path or PID, may be needed. I measured the cost on **vLLM 0.31.0**, using a 66-shard, approximately 28.75 GiB Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 checkpoint on OSSFS and one H20-3e GPU (TP=1). Both variants used the same live daemon, `ipc_cache`, `zero_copy`, `fallback=false`, and the same warm compilation caches: - A: run the original `hash_checkpoint()` on every engine start. - B: reuse the fingerprint captured from that same daemon's initial computation, while retaining the other `WeightCacheKey` and GPU UUID checks. The runs were ordered A → B → B → A. | Variant | Checkpoint fingerprint | Model-loading stage | Total startup to `/health` 200 | | --- | ---: | ---: | --

title: Restore multimodal requests from processed state and existing KV
body: Provide a supported vLLM API to export the processed state of a multimodal prompt and restore it for continuation from existing KV, without loading or preprocessing the media again. If the KV covers the required image-dependent computation and the model's continuation state is available, the second instance should be able to continue generation using the exact token sequence, media identities, and layout established by the first instance. The input-state contract should be independent of a particular orchestrator or KV transport. vLLM already has relevant capabilities to build on: - [#52697](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/52697) allows KV consumers to omit multimodal embedding tensors through `allow_missing_mm_embeddings`. - [#54659](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/54659), which closed [#54658](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/54658), exposes `features.mm_metadata` separately from full tensor data in the Render/Generate protocol. - [#55639](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/55639) discusses using KV or embedding reuse to avoid redundant encoder work. title: vllm run-batch --resume to continue an interrupted batch
body: With #52505, `vllm run-batch` writes each response as soon as it finishes, so an interrupted run leaves the finished responses on disk. There is still no way to continue from there. The output file is opened with `"w"` when the run starts, so rerunning with the same `-o` truncates it and recomputes everything. In a test with 4000 requests on an A10G (#52505 head), a run killed after 1664 responses was rerun with the same `-o`, and the file was back to 0 lines as soon as the writer opened it. This matters most where batch jobs get interrupted routinely: spot or preemptible instances, Kubernetes evictions, Slurm preemption, or one bad node in a large sharded job. Today the options are to redo the whole shard or filter the input by hand. Proposal: a `--resume` flag. When it is set and the local output file exists: 1. Read the existing output and collect the `custom_id`s that have a 200 response. Lines with an error status are retried, since some of them are not real failures (see below). 2. Drop a trailing line that isn't valid JSON. A SIGKILL can land in the middle of a write. I didn't hit this with ~4 KB responses, but large responses make it more likely. 3. Open the file in append mode and dispatch only the requests that are left. 4. Fail before the model loads if the input has duplicate `custom_id`s. `BatchRequestInput` already says they "Must be unique for each request in a batch", but nothing checks it, and resume can't be correct without it. `validate_batch` already parses every line before the engine starts, so the check is cheap. Scope would be local output files. A URL output is only uploaded when the run succeeds, so there is nothing partial to resume from. - A wrapper script that filters the input against the old output and appends to it. It works, but everyone ends up writing their own, and it has to know the error-line caveat below. - Writing errors to a separate file, like the OpenAI Batch API's error file, would make "what is left" easier to compute, bu

title: Slow EngineCore/worker teardown leaves VRAM held after shutdown, so the next engine fails its startup memory check
body: On ROCm, after a vLLM engine is shut down, its GPU memory can stay held for tens of seconds. Anything that starts a new engine shortly after stopping one then fails the startup memory check: ValueError: Free memory on device cuda:0 (171.76/191.98 GiB) on startup is less than desired GPU memory utilization (0.92, 176.63 GiB). **Where it has been seen** 1. AMD CI, `(MI300) LM Eval Small Models Harness - The test runs 6 models back to back in one pytest process. - Model 5's EngineCore got SIGTERM at 09:22:27 and model 6 started at 09:22:30. - At model 6's memory check (09:22:56, 29 s after SIGTERM), about 20 GiB was still in use. - Models 1–5 each started with 191.46 GiB free. **Possibly related:** in the same CI build, `(MI300) Distributed Torchrun + Shutdown` hung for 2400 s in `v1/shutdown/test_startup_error.py::test_async_llm_startup_error[forward-2-...]`. The EngineCore logged "EngineCore failed to start" and "all workers exited gracefully", but its process never exited, so `wait_for_engine_startup` kept polling. This has not reproduced locally (43 runs, with and without CPU load). - **Larger allocations to free:** at 0.92 utilization an engine holds about 176 GiB on MI300X and about 265 GiB on MI355X, mostly KV cache. - **Spawn vs fork exit path:** ROCm uses spawn. Spawned children exit through `sys.exit()`, which runs full interpreter finalization (`atexit` handlers including torch/HIP, GC, finalizers). Forked children exit via `os._exit()` and skip all of that. Slow or hanging `atexit` work would delay process exit and therefore VRAM release. This would also explain the torch 2.13 zombie report. - **Asynchronous VRAM release in the driver:** the amdgpu driver can free VRAM after the process exits. Existing vLLM comments already note this (`VllmRunner.__exit__`, `get_engine_process_shutdown_timeout` in `vllm/v1/engine/utils.py`). - **Grace period:** `ROCM_ENGINE_PROCESS_SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT_S = 15.0` only applies when both the request timeout and the process timeout

title: Per-request prefix-cache miss attribution (prompt divergence vs. eviction)
body: Automatic prefix caching is one of the biggest cost and latency wins for RAG and agent workloads, where every request re-sends a long, mostly identical scaffold (system prompt, tool schemas, few-shot examples). vLLM already reports per-request cached tokens (`num_cached_tokens`, `usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens`), so you can tell roughly *where* the cache hit ended. What you can't tell is what happened to the first block after the hit. Users typically care about two common causes, which need very different fixes: - **The prompt changed.** A timestamp or request ID in the system prompt, tool definitions serialized in a different order, a user name injected near the top. Each one invalidates every block after it. The fix is in the application. - **The block was evicted.** The prefix was cached earlier but got pushed out under memory pressure. The fix is capacity, routing or cache offload, not the prompt. vLLM can't infer the cause. The diagnostic below reports what it observed and leaves the interpretation to the user. Today both look identical from the outside: a short cache hit. Telling them apart means diffing tokenized prompts by hand and guessing about eviction. **Proposal:** optional per-request diagnostics, disabled by default: - a **miss reason** for the first uncached block after the longest hit: `evicted` (its hash was cached and evicted recently: with the flag on, hashes dropped in `BlockPool._maybe_evict_cached_block` are also recorded as `BlockHashWithGroupId` in a fixed-size LRU, e.g. sized to `num_gpu_blocks`, roughly one cache turnover; a hit there is definite) or `no_match` (not seen within that window: a changed prompt, a never-seen prompt, or an eviction older than the window; ambiguous by design). `no_match` covers both changed prompt tokens and changed extra keys mixed into the block hash (`cache_salt`, LoRA adapter, multimodal inputs), so on its own it is not proof that the text changed. - a third outcome, `lookup_limit`, when the hit l

title: Support trainer-side pipeline parallelism with NCCL M2N weight transfer
body: PR [[#51520] adds NCCL M2N weight transfer for resharing trainer weights directly into vLLM workers. The current M2N source contract requires every trainer rank to follow the same parameter manifest and participate in every parameter transfer. This does not represent pipeline parallelism greater than one, where each pipeline stage owns only part of the model: In current vLLM `main`, the trainer integration must first normalize this stage-local ownership into the complete named-tensor stream expected by the weight-update interface. This can require additional collection or forwarding before transfer. The requested feature is to let M2N transfer each parameter directly from its owning pipeline-stage ranks: All participants must still agree on a global parameter order and transfer plan before NCCL initialization to prevent mismatched collectives. This is needed for models that require PP>1 to fit and to avoid unnecessary trainer-side gathering or relaying. The solution should be independent of the model, trainer framework, and number of pipeline stages. This issue will be related to issue #46429 to generalize for more models _No response_ _No response_

title: Support fused MoE weights with NCCL M2N weight transfer
body: In current vLLM main, online weight updates use the regular model-loading path for fused MoE weights: This path is correct because the model loader understands expert ownership and the runtime-specific fused representation. However, every generator worker receives the complete logical expert weights before selecting the experts it owns. PR [#51520](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51520) adds NCCL M2N weight transfer so trainer shards can be resharded directly into their destination layouts. Ordinary parameters can therefore avoid the existing full-tensor distribution path. Fused MoE parameters cannot use a simple direct destination because their source names and layouts do not directly correspond to the runtime tensors. For example, separate gate and up projections may need to be combined into w13_weight, and each expert-parallel worker owns only a subset of the global experts. As a result, these weights must still use the full-tensor fallback from PR #51520: This feature is requested so NCCL M2N can transfer only the expert data required by each destination worker while preserving the existing model-loader behavior for expert mapping, fusion, validation, and backend-specific packing. The desired result is: The solution should apply generally to fused MoE models and expert-parallel configurations. Unsupported layouts can continue using the full-tensor fallback. _No response_ _No response_

title: Logprobs on parsed path streaming `/derender`
body: Streaming `/derender` with a reasoning or tool parser (#50550) doesn't return logprobs. #55029 added streaming logprobs but only on the unparsed path. The parsed path builds its stream choices without them. A client that streams with `logprobs: true` through a parser gets nothing back. Agreed on #47161 (https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/47161#issuecomment-5893681568): the engine is the reference for logprob token strings. Standalone `/derender`, including the parsed path should use one shared resolver built on `convert_ids_list_to_tokens` and `_correct_decoded_token` with parity tests against the engine. Scope: - Resolve each chunk's logprobs and attach them to whatever delta the parser emits. `/v1/chat/completions` does the same, with one `logprobs.content` list no matter which field the tokens land in. - Update `logprob_context_token_ids` on the parsed path, like the plain path does. Keep it starting empty, like the engine. - Drop logprobs on every chunk when `include_reasoning=false` with a parser, like the engine does. - Fix batch derender too. `_derender_chat` clears `reasoning` but still returns the logprobs. - Add parity tests against `/v1/chat/completions` with `include_reasoning` on and off, a chunk the parser swallows (tool-call markup) and a multi-byte char split across chunks. `DerenderStreamState` stays as is. Chunk logprobs already cover only that chunk's tokens and replay never touches them, so no cursor is needed. #59510 handles streaming stop with a 400, so no pending text field either. ~Blocked on #58181 (still open).~ The shared helper (`decode_token_ids`) and the parity tests depend on it. @shimib has offered to take this. @hyeongyun0916 will review and help with repros. Re-resolving token strings separately in the parsed path. We ruled this out on #47161 because the paths already disagree (see #59241). - #47161: RFC thread where this was agreed - #55029: streaming logprobs for the unparsed path - #50550: parser aware streaming derender

title: shechduling using predicted decode output length
body: When prompts are long and concurrency is high, the scheduler can admit more requests than the KV cache can hold once decoding grows. A request then gets preempted and must be recomputed, which hurts performance. This is especially costly in prefill/decode disaggregation. If the decode instance is under too much KV pressure and has to recompute, that raises TPOT on the decode instance and lowers throughput for the whole system. `--watermark` can keep a fraction of the KV cache free and reduce this churn, but it is not flexible. It is a single value set at startup and cannot adapt to different workloads or to individual queries. In some workloads the service already knows the average output length, or an external model can cheaply estimate it. If that estimate is passed into the vLLM scheduler, admission can reserve KV cache for the prompt plus the estimated output, instead of only for the tokens needed right now. That should lower the chance of preemption. I can open a PR for this if it looks useful. thanks _No response_ _No response_

title: Helm chart: add an optional ServiceMonitor with a configurable regex filter to reduce the number of exported metrics
body: vLLM exposes a very large number of time series on its `/metrics` endpoint, and there is currently no simple way to limit them when deploying with the Helm chart in `examples/deployment/chart-helm`. The chart does not ship a `ServiceMonitor`, so users who collect vLLM metrics through a `ServiceMonitor`-compatible operator have to write their own, and in practice they end up ingesting everything. Most deployments only use a small subset of these metrics in their dashboards and alerts. The volume mainly comes from: - **Histograms.** Each histogram (end-to-end latency, time to first token, inter-token latency, prompt and generation lengths, prefill and decode times, ...) produces one `_bucket` series per bucket, plus `_sum` and `_count`. This is then multiplied by the number of replicas. - **Metrics that do not apply to a given deployment.** Depending on the setup, speculative decoding, LoRA or prefix cache metrics may never be used. - **Default Python client metrics.** The `python_*` and `process_*` families are exported by default and are rarely needed. At scale this increases scrape size, ingestion rate, storage and query cost in the metrics backend, for series that nobody queries. With several replicas, the cost grows linearly with the number of pods. You can measure the breakdown by metric family on any instance with: Add an optional `ServiceMonitor` template to the Helm chart, disabled by default so that current behavior does not change. It would expose the usual scrape settings (port, path, interval) and, most importantly, a way to filter metrics with regular expressions on the metric name, applied at collection time. Two modes would cover the common needs: - **Allowlist**: keep only the metrics whose name matches a regex. This is the most effective way to reduce the number of series, since anything not explicitly listed is dropped, including the default Python and process metrics. - **Denylist**: drop the metrics whose name matches a regex, for users who prefer

title: Add lifecycle management hooks for the worker extension class (--worker-extension-cls)
body: vLLM provides the` --worker-extension-cls` argument, which allows users to pass in a custom class that is injected as a base class of the worker abstraction. However, in` vllm/v1/worker/worker_base.py`, the current implementation only sets up the inheritance relationship — it does not define or invoke any lifecycle management interfaces. For example, there is no initialization hook being called, which means the actually running GPUWorker has no chance to initialize the injected functionality. While it is possible to invoke methods on the engine through /collective_rpc, this is not a good solution for lifecycle hooks such as an initializer or a destructor: * The caller has to trigger them manually at the right time, which is error-prone; * Initialization/cleanup are semantically tied to the worker's own construction and teardown, not to an ad-hoc RPC from the client side; * The extension itself has no way to guarantee its initialization runs before any other injected method is used. **Proposal**: define a set of extension lifecycle interfaces (e.g., `init_worker_extension`, and symmetrically something like `destroy_worker_extension`), and invoke them at the corresponding points of the worker lifecycle. For example, in `WorkerWrapperBase.init_worker`: With this in place, an extension class can optionally implement init_worker_extension() (and potentially a matching teardown hook), and vLLM will call it automatically at the right point of the worker lifecycle — no manual RPC needed. 1. **Calling the init/destroy functions via `/collective_rpc`**. This works mechanically, but lifecycle hooks invoked over RPC are detached from the worker's actual construction and destruction. Every client has to know about the hook and remember to call it in the right order, and there is no guarantee the extension is initialized before its other methods are invoked. 2. **Subclassing `GPUWorker` or monkey-patching it in downstream projects**. title: Dynamic Latent-Trajectory Consensus Governor for Reasoning Models (DeepSeek-R1 / QwQ) to Free KV-Cache 4.5x Faster
body: Research paper : [SubNeutralize__The_Geometry_of_Reasoning_and_the_Elimination_of_the_Overthinking_Trap (4) (1).pdf](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/32702285/SubNeutralize__The_Geometry_of_Reasoning_and_the_Elimination_of_the_Overthinking_Trap.4.1.pdf) Autoregressive reasoning models (e.g., `DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B`, `QwQ-32B`) present a massive throughput bottleneck in vLLM: * In up to 40% of coding and reasoning tasks, models derive the correct solution within early generation (80–120 tokens). * Instead of emitting the final answer, the model enters repetitive post-deduction monologue loops ("Wait, let me double check... what if null? Actually, step 1 was right..."), consuming 1,500+ tokens. * **The vLLM Impact:** This unnecessarily occupies PagedAttention KV-cache slots for 2+ minutes per sequence, starving the scheduler, inflating queues, and degrading global serving throughput. --- Rather than applying arbitrary token limits or heuristic string parsing, we propose an early-exit mechanism (**SubNeutralize**) computed directly from latent trajectory dynamics at the model's cognitive bottleneck layer (layer 14 on 1.5B/7B, layer 32 on 32B). title: Add configurable startupProbe for slow model initialization
body: The Helm chart currently provides readiness and liveness probes against `/health`, but does not provide a startup probe. The default liveness probe is configured as follows: With the current defaults, consecutive liveness probe failures can trigger a container restart as early as roughly 35 seconds after container start. The exact timing may vary slightly depending on probe scheduling and timeouts. When starting large models, vLLM may perform several normal initialization steps, including: - Loading model checkpoints - Allocating the KV cache - Kernel compilation and autotuning - CUDA graph capture - Model-specific warmup These initialization steps can take substantially longer than 35 seconds. While `/health` is still unavailable during initialization, the liveness probe cannot distinguish normal slow startup from a startup that is genuinely stuck or unhealthy. As a result, a container that is still making normal initialization progress can be restarted repeatedly and may eventually enter `CrashLoopBackOff`. I propose adding the following startup probe as the default in `examples/deployment/chart-helm/values.yaml`: With these proposed defaults, the startup budget would be approximately 30 minutes: This default is intended to accommodate cold starts for large models while remaining configurable based on model size and initialization characteristics. A longer startup budget reduces the risk of prematurely restarting a container that is still making progress, but it also delays detection and recovery when startup is genuinely stuck. The main goal of this proposal is therefore not simply to increase a timeout, but to separate **startup lifecycle handling from runtime liveness detection**. The exact default `failureThreshold` can be adjusted based on maintainer feedback. Until the startup probe succeeds, Kubernetes does not execute the readiness or liveness probes. After startup succeeds, both probes run using their existing configurations. Users who do not need a start

title: Add calibrated FP8 KV-cache support for sparse MLA
body: While doing validation on https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/58056 I noticed that `tencent/Hy4-preview-FP8` provides FP8 weights but no calibrated FP8 KV-cache scales: When `--kv-cache-dtype fp8` is enabled, vLLM defaults the Q/K scales to `1.0`. This causes a large accuracy regression with `ROCM_AITER_MLA_SPARSE`. Matched 20-example GSM8K results: | KV-cache dtype | Accuracy | Truncated | |---|---:|---:| | BF16 (`auto`) | 95% | 5% | | FP8 | 50% | 40% | From a bit of digging, I think there are two options here: 1. **Static calibrated scales** (less work up front, but not necessary robust across workloads) - Calibrate and export per-layer Q and compressed-KV scales. - Load them following the Kimi K3 or DeepSeek V3.2 pattern. 2. **Dynamic block scales** (more impl work upfront, but scales to new workloads) - Add ROCm support for an embedded-scale format similar to `fp8_ds_mla`. - Compute per-token or per-block UE8M0 scales when writing the cache, following DeepSeek V4. cc: @akii96 Use `--kv-cache-dtype auto` so Hy4 keeps a BF16 KV cache. vLLM could also reject or require explicit opt-in for uncalibrated FP8 KV when the checkpoint declares `kv_cache_quant_algo: null`. - Hardware: 8× AMD Instinct MI350X (`gfx950`) - Parallelism: TP8 - Backend: `ROCM_AITER_MLA_SPARSE` - Model revision: `4215ec29de873a998e849cee902654490c7ff4d1` - vLLM commit: `79468c20ef23227d4e051f807e10fd54fb24e24f` - Related: #54594, #58056

title: instruction-preserving truncation for `/v1/chat/completions`, and document `truncate_prompt_tokens` semantics
body: **Motivation.** We run LLM-as-judge evaluation through `/v1/chat/completions`. Each request is a system message, a grading rubric, the question, the reference answer, and the candidate model's response. Occasionally a candidate degenerates into a repetition loop; one 1,854-token response became ~16k prompt tokens after JSON escaping and overflowed a 14,336-token judge (`"This model's maximum context length is 14336 tokens. However, your request has 15995 input tokens."`). The only server-side tool for this today is `truncate_prompt_tokens`, and for this prompt shape it is unusable: - It keeps the **last** k tokens of the rendered prompt (`vllm/sampling_params.py`: "will use only the last k tokens from the prompt (i.e., left truncation)"). The system message, rubric and question are at the front, so they are discarded first, and the judge is left grading the tail of the garbage response with no rubric and no reference. - For text inputs the actual side is not even guaranteed: the chat path tokenizes with `truncation=True, max_length=k`, and `vllm/inputs/preprocess.py` branches on `tokenizer.truncation_side`, so behavior depends on the model's tokenizer config. - None of this is in the OpenAI-compatible-server docs; the semantics live only in a `SamplingParams` docstring. Rubric-first, RAG-style and tool-instruction prompts all share this shape: the important tokens are at the start, the compressible tokens are in the middle. **Proposal.** 1. Add an opt-in, instruction-preserving truncation mode for chat completions. Two possible surfaces: - a `truncation: "auto" | "disabled"` field mirroring the Responses API, implemented item-aligned (drop whole non-system messages from the front, keep the system message and the last user message, never split a message); or - a per-message `truncate: true` marker so the client can designate exactly which message may be shortened (from its end) to fit. title: Attempts to avoid full promt processing when changing the tool set
body: I want (for example) to pass two hypothetical tools to the neural network: - Get temperature - Get time Further, during execution, I want to block individual calls and sometimes impose additional requirements on the output (for example, in XML format). The problem is that if I pass this in the tools field, the tools are simultaneously included in the chat-template and used as a grammar to restrict the output. If I change the set of tools, this leads to a complete recalculation of the context (and the model may have a slightly worse understanding of what was previously discussed without the tool descriptions). Also, if I ignore the tools field and pass the tools as chat-template-kwards, they are included in the system prompt, and if I pass them in structured_output, they are even included in the grammar to restrict the output. But then I have: 1. The generated results don't include native tool-calls; I have to write a parser myself. 2. I force the neural network to use the format I choose. For example, I'll describe the format as JSON, but qwen's native format is XML tags. It certainly works, but I'm not sure it's a good solution. So, there are three entities: 1 - tools in the chat-template, which is described in the system prompt. 2 - grammar for limiting the output 3 - output parser built into vllm (yes, each neural network series has its own, like gemma4). title: Recommended way to serve multiple models (e.g. embedding) on a single GPU
body: **Description:** We run vLLM to serve a small embedding model on a dedicated GPU. The model uses only a fraction of the GPU's memory and compute. We would like to co-locate several models on the same GPU to improve utilization. - A single vLLM process serves a single model. - The docs say `gpu_memory_utilization` is a per-instance limit, so several instances can share a GPU (e.g. 0.5 each). - Community answers say this works in online (server) mode, but not in offline mode with several `LLM` objects in one process (#6155). There is no official guidance on the recommended way to do this in production, in particular: 1. Is running several vLLM server instances on one GPU with split `--gpu-memory-utilization` values the officially recommended approach? body: Qwen3.8-27B on MI350P, vLLM 0.31.1rc1.dev88, AITER enabled. (a) AiterMxfp4LinearKernel quantizes activations in a separate kernel before each GEMM: 309 launches, 1.2 ms of a ~10.6 ms step at c=1 (decode TPOT 9.5 ms, mem% ~40%). gemm_with_dynamic_quant is opaque to the compiler even with fuse_norm_quant on. I'm serving Qwen3.8-27B (amd/Qwen3.8-27B-Quark-AWQ-MXFP4) on a single AMD Instinct MI350P (gfx950, 128 CUs) with vLLM 0.31.1rc1.dev88 (vllm/vllm-openai-rocm:nightly) for low-latency single-user and small-batch decode (c=1 to ~32), with image input enabled. title: Scheduler.schedule() is the most complex function in the codebase (complexity 136, 841 lines)

body: **Repo:** https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm **File issue:** https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/new --- | | | |---|---| | **vLLM** | 0.24.0 | | **Model** | `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash` | | **Hardware** | 2× NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition (96 GB each) | | **GPU architecture** | SM120 (compute capability 12.0) | | **Driver** | 595.71.05 (open kernel module) | | **CUDA** | 13.0 (toolkit & runtime) | | **Python** | 3.12 | | **OS** | Ubuntu 24.04 | --- Launching with the default `--kv-cache-dtype auto` (or omitting the flag entirely, which is equivalent) crashes vLLM during model initialisation: The HuggingFace model page shows: …with no `--kv-cache-dtype` flag. This works on H100/SM100 but silently fails on Blackwell SM120 — there is no hint in the error message that `--kv-cache-dtype fp8` is required on this architecture. vLLM then auto-upgrades `fp8` → `fp8_ds_mla` internally. --- Two separate places in the codebase reject `auto` for SM120 without providing an auto-resolution path. On SM10x, `auto` falls through to the bfloat16 path. On SM120, `use_fp8_ds_mla_layout` is always `True`, so `auto` hits the assertion before any fallback is attempted. --- On SM120, `auto` should be silently resolved to `fp8_ds_mla`, parallel to how `auto` resolves to bfloat16 on SM10x. The user shouldn't need to know about SM120-specific memory layout internals to run a supported model on supported hardware. --- In `_resolve_dsv4_kv_cache_dtype` (`attention.py`): And in the SM12x branch of the validator (`flashinfer_sparse.py`), allow `auto` (or resolve it to `fp8_ds_mla` before the check): --- - There is a related issue: `VLLM_USE_DEEP_GEMM=1` (default) crashes during FP8 GEMM warmup on Blackwell for both DeepSeek-V4 and Qwen3.5 models. The workaround is `export VLLM_USE_DEEP_GEMM=0`. Separate report filed at [mix-labs/BUG-Report-vLLM-DeepGemm-Warmup.md](./BUG-Report-vLLM-DeepGemm-Warmup.md). - Tested on vLLM 0.24.0. title: vLLM 0.24.0 crashes on startup with Qwen3.6-27B-FP8 on Blackwell SM120 — DeepGemm warmup ignores auto-disable
body: - **vLLM**: 0.24.0 - **Model**: `Qwen/Qwen3.6-27B-FP8` (model_type: `qwen3_5_text`) - **Hardware**: 2x NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition (96 GB each) - **GPU Architecture**: SM120 (compute capability 12.0) - **Driver**: 595.71.05 (open kernel module) - **CUDA**: 13.0 (toolkit & runtime) - **PyTorch**: 2.11.0+cu130 - **OS**: Ubuntu 24.04 Starting vLLM 0.24.0 with Qwen3.6-27B-FP8 on Blackwell SM120 GPUs fails during the DeepGemm warmup phase with: The crash occurs in `_deepgemm_fp8_gemm_nt_warmup` during the FP8 GEMM warmup. vLLM 0.24.0 correctly **detects** that DeepGemm should be disabled for `qwen3_5_text` on Blackwell and logs: This sets `quant_config.use_deep_gemm = False` in `vllm/config/vllm.py:925`. However, the FP8 GEMM warmup code in `model_executor/warmup/deep_gemm_warmup.py` checks `envs.VLLM_USE_DEEP_GEMM` (the environment variable, defaulting to `True`) **instead** of the `quant_config.use_deep_gemm` flag. As a result, the warmup still attempts to run DeepGemm kernels and crashes. The server will crash during startup. Setting `VLLM_USE_DEEP_GEMM=0` before starting vLLM resolves the issue: The server starts normally with CUTLASS fallback and all features working. The auto-disable logic in `vllm/utils/deep_gemm.py::should_auto_disable_deep_gemm()` should propagate through to the warmup path, so that FP8 GEMM warmup respects the `quant_config.use_deep_gemm = False` flag and skips DeepGemm warmup entirely for affected model/arch combinations. In `vllm/model_executor/warmup/deep_gemm_warmup.py`, the warmup function should check the `quant_config.use_deep_gemm` flag (or the auto-disable result) in addition to `envs.VLLM_USE_DEEP_GEMM`, or the env var should be set to `0` when auto-disable triggers. - `vllm/config/vllm.py:925` — sets `quant_config.use_deep_gemm = False` with warning - `vllm/utils/deep_gemm.py:33` — `should_auto_disable_deep_gemm()` correctly identifies the model - `vllm/model_executor/warmup/deep_gemm_warmup.py` — warmup checks

title: Serving the model opt Quantized W8A8
body: Currently, vLLM features robust INT8 / W8A8 execution paths underneath (leveraging CUTLASS kernels), but the configuration loader inside vllm/model_executor/layers/quantization/modelopt.py restricts model ingestion heavily based on a strict whitelist. When a user tries to deploy a model that has been quantized to W8A8 (INT8 / SmoothQuant) using the NVIDIA ModelOpt library, vLLM throws a Pydantic ValidationError at runtime. The file modelopt.py only implements mapping abstractions for ModelOptFp8Config, ModelOptNvFp4Config, and ModelOptMxFp8Config. It completely lacks the configuration classes and tensor translation logic necessary to recognize a ModelOpt INT8 configuration setup. While tools like llm-compressor work out of the box with the compressed-tensors loader standard, teams deploying models originating from NVIDIA-native frameworks (which export checkpoints using quant_method: "modelopt" and quant_algo: "INT8") are entirely blocked from serving their models on vLLM. title: CPU source build fails on GCC < 15: sgl-kernels use AVX10.2 unconditionally
body: `cmake/cpu_extension.cmake` advertises `gcc/g++ >= 12.3` as the requirement for the x86 CPU backend, but `csrc/cpu/sgl-kernels` has used AVX10.2 unconditionally since #49942. AVX10.2 support (the `target("avx10.2")` attribute, the fp8 convert intrinsics, and the `__builtin_cpu_supports("avx10.2")` argument) only arrived in GCC 15. On any older compiler this is not a missing fast path, it is a hard build failure: Five objects fail to compile, so a CPU source build is broken on every current distro default toolchain: Ubuntu 24.04 (gcc 13), Debian 12 (gcc 12), RHEL 9 (gcc 11). CI does not catch this because `docker/Dockerfile.cpu` installs `gcc-15` from a PPA, so the only compiler the CPU jobs ever see is one that supports AVX10.2. The AVX10.2 code is already an opportunistic fast path: both call sites in `gemm_fp8_w8a8.cpp` are guarded at runtime by `if (avx10_2_available())` with the AVX512 loop immediately below, and that AVX512 loop is what every non-Diamond-Rapids machine executes today. So the fix is to probe for `-mavx10.2` at configure time and compile the AVX10.2 helpers only when the compiler can express them, mirroring the existing `-mamx-fp8` probe a few lines above in the same file.
label: installation

title: v0.30.0 CPU wheels now require manylinux_2_39 (glibc 2.39), breaking installation on Ubuntu 22.04/Rhel9
body: - OS: Ubuntu 22.04 LTS (glibc 2.35) / Rhel9.6 (glibc 2.34) - Arch: x86_64 - Python: 3.10 - Installing: `vllm-0.30.0+cpu-cp38-abi3-manylinux_2_39_x86_64.whl` from the GitHub release assets Hi vLLM team (@khluu (release coordinator of v0.30.0), @bigPYJ1151 (reviewer of [PR49410](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/49410)), @zhejiangxiaomai (author of [PR49410](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/49410))), first of all, thank you for the v0.30.0 release and for continuing to ship prebuilt CPU wheels. They are very helpful for us. We noticed that the platform tag of the CPU wheels changed between releases: | Release | CPU wheel platform tag | |---|---| | v0.29.0 | `manylinux_2_34` (x86_64 / aarch64) | | v0.30.0 | `manylinux_2_39` (x86_64 / aarch64) | From what we can tell, this comes from `docker/Dockerfile.cpu` moving its base image from `ubuntu:22.04` (GCC 12) to `ubuntu:25.04` (GCC 15) in #49410, which was needed for the binutils >= 2.44 requirement of the new AMX-FP8 kernels. The CUDA (`manylinux_2_28`) and XPU (`manylinux_2_34`) wheels were not affected. As a result, the official CPU wheels can no longer be installed on Ubuntu 22.04 LTS (glibc 2.35) and Rhel9 (glibc 2.34). Ubuntu 22.04 is still within Canonical's standard support window (until April 2027, with ESM until 2032) and is still widely used in production and CI environments, including ours. We could not find any note in the release notes or docs indicating that dropping Ubuntu 22.04 / glibc < 2.39 support for CPU wheels was intended, so we wanted to raise it here. Would it be possible to continue publishing a CPU wheel that is installable on Ubuntu 22.04 (glibc 2.35), for example with a `manylinux_2_34` tag, alongside the new `manylinux_2_39` wheel? We would be happy to help test a candidate wheel on Ubuntu 22.04, or to contribute a PR for the build change if the maintainers agree on a direction. Thank you for your time and for all the work on vLLM!

title: q_gemm.cu fails to compile: missing half and half2 atomicAdd overloads
body: (`collect_env.py` was run after the build succeeded with the workaround below, which is why a vLLM version is reported at all.) The compiler and HIP headers come from the TheRock per-architecture wheels at `https://rocm.nightlies.amd.com/v2/gfx1151/` (`rocm-sdk-core`, `rocm-sdk-devel`, `rocm-sdk-libraries-gfx1151`, 7.13.0a20260424), installed into the venv; `ROCM_PATH` / `HIP_PATH` point at `<venv>/lib/python3.13/site-packages/_rocm_sdk_devel`. No system ROCm is involved. Building vLLM `v0.26.0` (`568afb3a1`) from source for gfx1151 fails in `q_gemm.cu` with ten `no matching function for call to 'atomicAdd'` errors. The HIP headers in the TheRock 7.13 nightly SDK used here do not provide the `__half` and `__half2` overloads called by this file. The build uses a Python 3.13 venv with the gfx1151 torch 2.11.0 wheel already installed. The following command is reconstructed from `build_env.sh` and the build log; the exact original invocation was not recorded: Ninja fails while compiling the GPTQ object for `_C_stable_libtorch`: Eight errors are calls to `atomicAdd` on `half2*` at generated `.hip` lines 319, 320, 436, 437, 560, 561, 680, and 681. The other two are calls on `half*` at lines 1269 and 1357. These correspond to lines 318–319, 435–436, 559–560, 679–680, 1268, and 1356 in the unpatched v0.26.0 `q_gemm.cu`. `csrc/libtorch_stable/quantization/gptq/q_gemm.cu` is part of `VLLM_STABLE_EXT_SRC`, which is built for both CUDA and HIP (`CMakeLists.txt:384`). title: VLLM_PRECOMPILED_WHEEL_COMMIT=nightly is rejected
body: The installation documentation states that `VLLM_PRECOMPILED_WHEEL_COMMIT=nightly` selects the latest already-built wheel. The installation then falls back to a recent main-branch commit. When the wheel for that commit is not available yet, the installation fails with an HTTP 404 error. The special `nightly` value should be preserved so that the most recent already-built wheel is selected. The source checkout under test is `vllm-project/vllm` main at commit `6f00a1a`. The relevant validation in `setup.py` currently accepts only values whose length is 40, despite the installation documentation also allowing the special value `nightly`.

title: ROCm install silently falls back to CUDA abi3 wheel on Python < 3.12 (no ROCm abi3 / cp311 / cp313 wheels)
body: > **Note on the `collect_env` ROCm version:** `collect_env` reports `ROCM Version: 5.2.21153-0`, but the active runtime on this host is ROCm 7.2 (`PyTorch version: 2.12.0+rocm7.2`, `ROCM used to build PyTorch: 7.2.53211`, `HIP runtime version: 7.2.53211`, `rocm-core 7.2.0`, `/opt/rocm-7.2.0`). The `5.2` string comes from a Debian-packaged `/usr/bin/hipconfig` (5.2-era) that shadows the 7.2 install on `PATH`. This is incidental and does not affect the finding, the `vLLM Build Flags: ROCm: Disabled` line holds regardless of which ROCm version is installed. When installing vLLM on an AMD/ROCm host running Python 3.11 via the `--extra-index-url` method from the [vLLM release page](https://vllm.ai/releases), the resolver silently installs the **CUDA** wheel instead of failing or installing a ROCm artifact. Root cause: the ROCm index at `https://wheels.vllm.ai/rocm/vllm/` currently provides only **cp312** wheels: Because there is no `abi3` / `cp311` / `cp313` ROCm wheel, a resolver running on Python 3.11 rejects the `cp312` ROCm artifact on ABI grounds. Since `--extra-index-url` *merges* the custom index with PyPI (rather than replacing it), the resolver then falls back to the standard PyPI release, `vllm-0.22.1-cp38-abi3-manylinux_2_28_x86_64.whl`. Its `cp38-abi3` tag is a valid match for Python 3.11, so it installs cleanly, but vLLM's PyPI wheels are compiled for **CUDA**, so an AMD host silently ends up with a CUDA build. Net effect: users on AMD hardware running the distro-default Python (e.g. Python 3.11 on Debian 12 Bookworm) who omit the strict `+rocm722` local version string unknowingly install a CUDA wheel that cannot load on their GPU. Pinning `vllm==0.22.1+rocm722` instead produces a clear `No matching distribution found` on Python 3.11 i.e. the failure is silent only because the local-version tag was omitted. Running on Python 3.11 installs `vllm-0.22.1-cp38-abi3-manylinux_2_28_x86_64.whl` (note: no `+rocm` local version tag). Its bundled `.so` files expose it

title: Skip gaps in sliding-window prefix-cache hit search
body: `SlidingWindowManager.find_longest_cache_hit` currently scans every block from right to left, costing up to `max_num_blocks` `BlockPool.get_cached_block` lookups even when the cache is cold. Sliding-window groups commonly run at a low hit rate, so a 128K-token request with a 4K window performs ~8192 lookups (block_size=16) although a hit only needs `cdiv(sliding_window - 1, block_size) = 256` contiguous blocks. The function already carries a TODO for this. Proposed change: probe every `stride = sliding_window_contiguous_blocks`-th block from the right. Every candidate run of `stride` cached blocks contains exactly one probe, so the lattice cannot skip a hit. On a probe hit, expand to the right (at most `stride - 1` blocks, since the next probe missed), verify only windows containing the probe, and after a miss at `idx` resume at the next aligned edge below `idx - 1`. Alignment retries advance by `alignment_tokens // gcd(alignment_tokens, block_size)` blocks, and the cached-prefix fallback is computed directly. Function-level measurements (`find_longest_cache_hit`, block_size=16, sliding_window=4096, 128K tokens, alignment=16, no EAGLE, single-thread CPU): | pattern | main lookups | proposed lookups | main time | proposed time | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:| | cold cache | 8192 | 33 | 4.49 ms | 0.021 ms | | 1% random cached | 8192 | 33 | 4.61 ms | 0.021 ms | | tail hit / full cache | 256 | 257 | 0.23 ms | 0.23 ms | | adversary (cached blocks on the probe lattice) | 8192 | 128 | 4.63 ms | 0.11 ms | The worst case remains O(max_num_blocks), but the common low-hit-rate case becomes O(max_num_blocks / stride), and the measured adversarial case is still well below the current full scan. _No response_ - Every probe hit triggers right-expansion and verification bounded to windows containing the probe, so gaps are skipped regardless of which side the miss is on. - Alignment retries jump by the alignment period, covering hybrid models where `alignment_tokens != block_size`. - The

title: Resize video frames while decoding to skip full-resolution copies
body: **TL;DR:** Resize video frames right after decoding instead of in the HF processor. For Qwen3-VL on 1080p video: 10–60× smaller frame arrays, 35–46% less decode + processor time, 1.8–2.5× throughput when preprocessing-bound, and `pixel_values_videos` stays bit-identical. **Problem.** vLLM's video loaders keep every sampled frame at full resolution; the HF processor then copies and resizes them. Most video processors downscale (Qwen2.5-VL, Qwen3-VL, GLM-4.xV, LLaVA-OneVision, InternVL, ...). For Qwen3-VL, a 5-min 1080p video at 2 fps is 600 frames ≈ 3.5 GiB per request, resized down to 256×128 (W×H). **Proposal.** Resize each frame right after decoding, using the same op and target size as the HF processor (Qwen3-VL: torchvision bicubic + antialias on uint8, size from `smart_resize`). The processor then computes the same target size from the already-resized frames, so its resize changes nothing and `pixel_values_videos` is bit-identical. That holds for common aspect ratios but not always (e.g. 480×1920 with ≥258 frames shrinks one more step), so the loader checks it and otherwise keeps the current path. The resize is generic; each model only supplies its target size. Starting with Qwen3-VL, the only one measured so far. **Results** (Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct, Big Buck Bunny 1080p h264, RTX 4090 + 16 vCPU EPYC 7542; OpenCV decode backend, fps=2; bit-identical on both clips): | Video | Frame array (MiB) | Decode + processor (s) | req/s, c=4 | req/s, c=8 | |---|---|---|---|---| | 60 s (120 frames) | 712 → 67 | 3.84 → 2.51 | 0.37 → 0.68 | 0.33 → 0.65 | | 300 s (600 frames) | 3560 → 56 | 15.5 → 8.31 | 0.10 → 0.23 | 0.11 → 0.27 | - The 300 s clip ends up smaller because Qwen3-VL caps total pixels across all frames, so frames shrink as the frame count grows (120 frames → 608×320, 600 frames → 256×128). - Memory and time columns: one process, no engine, 1 torch thread, median of 3 (the repro script below). - Throughput columns: `vllm serve` with the change applied as a runtime pa

title: Reduce load_weights synchronization overhead for DeepSeek V4 Flash weight updates on H200
body: Profiling repeated weight updates for **DeepSeek V4 Flash on NVIDIA H200** revealed substantial CPU waiting and accounting overhead inside `load_weights`. The transfer method involves sorting all weights by layer into buckets of ≤8 GB, with each bucket triggering a `load_weights` operation. For the second `load_weights` invocation in each trace, the combined experimental optimizations reduced profiled CPU duration from **1,923.691 ms to 276.823 ms**, an **85.61% reduction / 6.95× speedup**. **Original loading flow** The baseline follows the existing layerwise reload path: 1. `load_weights` routes incoming weight names to parameters, shards, and experts. 2. `online_process_loader` buffers weights and calls `get_numel_loaded` to track layer completion. Accounting executes the original loader against meta parameters under `CopyCounter`. 3. Once a layer is ready, `_layerwise_process` materializes its parameters and replays the buffered loaders for actual loading. 4. Quantization post-processing prepares MXFP4 MoE weights for Marlin: repack `w13` and `w2`, then permute and encode their scales per expert. 5. Processed values are copied into the existing kernel tensor storage. Accounting and actual loading are interleaved as layers become ready. Expert ID mapping occurs in both paths. **Bottlenecks and implemented optimizations** 1. **GPU scalar reads during expert ID mapping** The baseline reads `expert_map[global_id].item()` from a GPU tensor for host-side decisions.
