title: Hybrid Mamba prefix caching (`mamba_cache_mode="align"`) costs 11-16% throughput on Nemotron-3.5-Lightning with no cache hits: per-group eager block-table ops, per-step align kernels outside CUDA graphs, and block-boundary prefill splits
body: Turning on prefix caching for a hybrid Mamba2 model forces `mamba_cache_mode="align"` (`vllm/model_executor/models/config.py:640-656`; since https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/58997 the only modes are `none` and `align`). On NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-NVFP4 (4x GB200, DP4/EP4, Model Runner V2), with a random 8K-in / 1K-out workload where nothing ever hits the cache, align mode costs: - **Output throughput: -13.4% to -16.2%** (median of 6 paired rounds, c=1/8/32/64). - **TPOT: +14% to +20%** from align mode itself, independent of block size and of prefill splitting. The decode step has **28 extra eager launches**: 4 Mamba KV-cache groups x 7 torch ops in `mamba_get_block_table_tensor`. The V2 align pre-process / pre-copy / post-process kernels also run every step outside the CUDA graph. GPU compute per step is unchanged; **GPU idle time per step grows by 0.55-0.75 ms**. - **TTFT at c=1: x1.8** (125 -> 229 ms). The scheduler splits an 8192-token prompt at the block boundary (4176 + 4016), and each prefill step carries 70-90 ms of fixed non-GPU cost, which is now paid twice. - Block size and KV capacity are **not** the cause. With prefix caching off, changing the block size to 6768 or 8192 stays within run-to-run noise. All configurations have >= 576x max concurrency and zero preemptions. With `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1`, prefix caching for Mamba2 is currently rejected at startup. A two-line fix (copy all 5 exact-replay states in align mode) makes hits and misses bitwise equal to prefix caching off. The extra copy costs about 9.4 us per step. That fix is not a PR yet; see the batch-invariance section below. This issue collects the measurements, the root cause and what the open PRs cover, so that someone can pick up the remaining work. - Hardware: 1 node, 4x NVIDIA GB200 (NVLink). - Model: `nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-NVFP4` (ModelOpt mixed precision: W4A16 NVFP4 routed and shared experts and lm_head, FP8 Mamba in_proj/out_proj). 23 Mamba

title: Octave KV, a native 3-bit KV cache for AMD GPUs
body: PR: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/59774 We serve Qwen3.8-27B (GPTQ W4A16) on boxes with four RX 7900 XTX, 96 GB in total, with tensor parallel 4 and MTP. Our users send long prompts: whole repositories, long documents, agent sessions that run for hours. With an fp16 KV cache and 8 GB per GPU for it, a box holds about 446k tokens, so one long request fills it. On ROCm today the options below 8 bits are TurboQuant, UltraQuant (#57057, gfx950 only) and KVarN (#46613, CUDA-first). We tried TurboQuant first, since it is merged and its idea (random rotation plus a Lloyd-Max codebook) is the right one. On our hardware three things got in the way: - With MTP on (`qwen3_next_mtp`, k=3) every preset produced garbage, and GSM8K fell to around 1%. Without MTP it was correct. - Its multi-token path copies between host and device per layer, so it cannot be captured in CUDA graphs. - Its Triton kernels are slow on RDNA3. At 380k tokens the first token took 621 s, against 371 s with fp16. So we wrote our own backend: same family of ideas, a few changes to the format, and every kernel in HIP. Against TurboQuant on the same hardware it comes out ahead on all three things we care about. It holds as many tokens or more at each size: at about 200 bytes per slot the two hold 2.07M and 2.05M tokens, and our 216-byte format holds 6% more than TurboQuant's 230-byte one. It loses less: 2.5× less excess NLL at 380k at the same size, and GSM8K stays at fp16 level (91.8-92.4 against 89.8). And it is faster: per layer at 380k, decode is 4.6× faster, MTP verification 11×, a prefill chunk takes 30% less time, and the first token of a 380k prompt arrives 2.1× sooner. We have run it in production since October 2, 2026, and we would like to propose it upstream. We would also like it to be more than an RDNA3 side project: one compressed KV format for the whole AMD line, with a short written contract that says what each architecture needs to implement. title: Avoid runtime routed_scaling_factor multiply between all-reduce and GEMM (MoE)
body: On ROCm (confirmed on AMD Instinct MI350X / gfx950), for any MoE model that sets `apply_routed_scale_to_output=True`, `MoERunner.forward()` in `vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/runner/moe_runner.py` applies the model's `routed_scaling_factor` as a standalone elementwise multiply positioned directly between the routed-output all-reduce and the subsequent output-transform GEMM. Under `torch.compile`, this multiply compiles to its own kernel launch (`triton_poi_fused_mul_2` in the traces below), introducing a small but measurable stall on the critical path between a collective-communication op and a GEMM — exactly where launch/synchronization overhead is most expensive relative to useful work. This was identified during an MI350-vs-B200 comparative performance gap analysis: no equivalent stall was observed on B200 for the same workload, pointing at this as a ROCm/AITER-path-specific inefficiency rather than an architectural requirement of the model. In `MoERunner.forward()`, the following methods execute in this exact order: 1. `_maybe_reduce_routed_output_before_transform()` → calls `tensor_model_parallel_all_reduce(fused_output)` 2. `_maybe_reduce_shared_expert_output()` → separate reduce for the shared-expert path 3. `_maybe_apply_routed_scale_to_output()` → `fused_output *= self.routed_scaling_factor` (BF16/FP32 branch; the FP16 branch instead scales the shared-expert output inversely to avoid overflow) 4. `apply_routed_output_transform()` → the model's output-side projection (for NemotronH's latent-space MoE, this is `fc2_latent_proj`, a `ReplicatedLinear` projecting `moe_latent_size` back to `hidden_size`) 5. `_maybe_reduce_final_output()` Step 3 sits directly between step 1 (the all-reduce) and step 4 (the GEMM), matching the observed stall position exactly. title: FlashAttention backend rebuilds KV-cache views on every call (+~21 µs CPU/layer since #44455)
body: Cache the (canonicalized) views on the impl and reuse them while the same `kv_cache` tensor is passed in. On v0.30, a local patch doing this cuts TTFT p50 by 12–16%, and the outputs match an fp32 reference with no numerical change: Notes: - The identity check matters. `profile_cudagraph_memory` first binds a minimal KV cache (`_init_minimal_kv_cache_for_profiling`), runs attention on it, frees it, and then allocates the real one. A cache keyed only on the first call would keep pointing at freed memory. - There is precedent for this: `TritonAttentionImpl` already caches KV-scale views in `_k_scale_cache` / `_v_scale_cache` ([triton_attn.py#L383-L440](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/v0.30.0/vllm/v1/attention/backends/triton_attn.py#L383-L440)), and `_cleanup_profiling_kv_cache` clears them. The FA view cache could be cleared in the same place. It should also be kept per impl, not in a module-level dict, so that the replaced tensor is not kept alive. - Hybrid models (e.g. Qwen3.5) only get this cost on their `full_attention` layers. I'm happy to open a PR. title: DeepSeek-V3.2 under DCP: FP8 sparse attention processes other ranks' masked top-k slots on Hopper
body: With decode context parallelism (DCP), each rank holds 1/dcp of every request's KV cache. For DeepSeek-V3.2, `FlashMLASparseImpl._forward_fp8_kv_mixed_batch` filters the indexer's 2048-wide top-k row per rank with `triton_filter_and_convert_dcp_index(..., compact_valid_to_front=False)`: slots owned by other ranks become `-1`, and the FP8 FlashMLA kernel runs on the full 2048-wide row. The kernel's work follows the row width, not the number of valid slots, so about (dcp-1)/dcp of the slots each rank processes are masked (~75% at DCP4). Under DCP this path also runs the prefill rows. On Hopper this cannot be fixed in vLLM alone: the SM90 V3.2 sparse decode kernel asserts `topk_length == nullptr` and takes `topk` from `indices.size(-1)`. Slicing the compacted row to a fixed width is fast, but it drops tokens whenever a rank owns more slots than the width, so it is not exact. Proposal: 1. FlashMLA: let the SM90 V3.2 sparse decode kernel honor `topk_length`, as SM100 already does. The same kernel change is open upstream as deepseek-ai/FlashMLA#216. 2. FlashMLA: the lengths differ per layer, so every layer needs its own schedule plan, and FlashMLA's single-threaded planner (16-24 us per call on H20) eats much of the gain at small batch. Make the planner faster while producing identical plans. 3. vLLM: compact each rank's slots with the in-kernel compaction the trtllm-gen path already uses, pass their count as `topk_length` with one batch entry per token, and bump FlashMLA. On 8x H20 (TP8 + DCP4 + EP, V3.2, `fp8_ds_mla` KV cache, vLLM main), steps 1 and 3 cut the prefill time of fresh prompts by 24-28% and the decode step time by 3.9-8.3% at 16-32 concurrent requests, with the attended token set unchanged. At 8 requests the decode time is unchanged (-1.9% to +0.8%); with step 2 as well, the decode step time drops by 2.6-10.8% at every point measured. GSM8K accuracy is unchanged. title: V2 runner PP side streams make gfx1201 (RDNA4) forward ~2× slower; main-stream option fixes it
body: On AMD gfx1201 (Radeon AI PRO R9700), a stream of small kernels picks up about 17 µs per dispatch when two or more other HIP streams hold pending waits on it (default hardware-queue limit, graph mode). The driver/runtime side, with a framework-free HIP reproducer, is reported at https://github.com/ROCm/TheRock/issues/9297. The V2 GPU model runner creates exactly that situation on the last pipeline-parallel stage: - `PPHandler.broadcast()` (and the draft-token broadcast) in `vllm/v1/worker/gpu/pp_utils.py` runs `broadcast_stream.wait_stream(main_stream)` and then enqueues the sends on `broadcast_stream`. - The async output path copies results device-to-host on its own copy stream, which also waits on the main stream. So while the next step's graph runs, two side queues are waiting on the main stream. On gfx1201 that roughly doubles the time of the dispatch-heavy decode forward. The gfx1030 (V620) control was unaffected; NVIDIA was not tested. The setup was PP=3 and TP=1 with ranks on V620, V620 and R9700 (last rank). It used an MoE hybrid model with MTP2 speculative decoding, FULL HIP graphs and ROCm 7.14. | Configuration | R9700 forward (15 layers), median | Pipeline step period | Decode throughput | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | Side streams (default) | ~16.9–17.0 ms | ~56–58 ms | ~33 tok/s | | Last-rank sends and output copy on the main stream | 7.18–7.23 ms | 41.6–42.2 ms | 45.3–46.6 tok/s | Across 803 measured R9700 forward intervals with the change, every one was below 10 ms. title: Narrower KV tiles speed up Triton embedding/reranking attention on RDNA3/RDNA4
body: `context_attention_fwd` in `vllm/v1/attention/ops/triton_prefill_attention.py` launches `_fwd_kernel` with a square tile: That is one tile shape for every backend. It is a reasonable default on CDNA, but RDNA3/RDNA4 are wave32 with a much smaller LDS budget, which makes a 128-wide KV tile a poor fit. I have not profiled the stall reason, so treat the mechanism as a hypothesis; what is measured is that the narrower tile is faster everywhere I tested. There is currently no ROCm- or RDNA-specific handling anywhere in this kernel. This kernel is reached through `EncoderOnlyAttention` and non-causal pooling in the `TRITON_ATTN` and `ROCM_ATTN` backends, so the affected workloads are **embedding and reranking models on RDNA3 and RDNA4**. Generation prefill and decode use separate attention paths and are unaffected by this change. Call-count instrumentation records zero calls into this kernel for the generation model tested. `vit_attn_wrappers.py` can reach this kernel as well, but on RDNA it does not: `RocmPlatform.get_vit_attn_backend()` returns `FLASH_ATTN` when `on_gfx1x()` and otherwise falls back to `TORCH_SDPA`, so ViT is only affected if the backend is set explicitly. Narrowing **only** the KV tile to 32, leaving `BLOCK_M`, `num_warps` and `num_stages` at their current values, measured on W7900 (gfx1100) and R9700 (gfx1201), bf16, TP=1, at stock clocks: | | gfx1100 | gfx1201 | | --- | --- | --- | | kernel, median of 36 cells | **2.56x-2.67x** | **2.25x-2.30x** | | offline end-to-end embedding latency | **1.10x-1.23x** | 1.08x-1.12x | | serving throughput (`vllm bench serve`) | **1.17x-1.19x** | 1.03x-1.05x | The kernel figure covers all 9 head sizes in `get_supported_head_sizes()` crossed with all four mask modes the kernel exposes, at batch 4, sequence 2048, 12 query heads and 2 KV heads. title: 100x speedup in v1 prompt_logprobs: Triton _topk_log_softmax_kernel vs native PyTorch topk/logsumexp on long contexts
body: When scoring prompt logprobs on long sequences ($T=8,192, K=32$), vLLM v1's Triton kernels (`_topk_log_softmax_kernel` and `_ranks_kernel` in `vllm/v1/worker/gpu/sample/logprob.py`) take **16.8 seconds** per forward pass. Replacing these kernels with native PyTorch GPU primitives: reduces logprob extraction time from **16.8s to 0.12s–0.19s** (an **88x to 140x speedup**), increasing end-to-end token scoring throughput from ~450 tok/s to **>5,000 tok/s**. - **GPU**: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 (24 GB) - **Model**: Llama-3.1-8B geometry ($V = 128,256$) - **Sequence Length**: 8,192 prompt tokens - **Requested Logprobs**: Top-32 (`prompt_logprobs=32`) | Component | Default Triton Implementation | PyTorch `torch.topk` + `torch.logsumexp` | Speedup | |---|---|---|---| | **Chunk 0:1024** | ~2.10s | 0.012s | **175x** | | **Full 8k Prompt Logprobs** | **16.80s** | **0.13s–0.19s** | **~100x** | | **Total Request Latency** | 18.2s (~450 tok/s) | 1.61s (~5,087 tok/s) | **11.3x** | 1. title: AWQ CUDA GEMM kernel is heavily L1/Memory bound (Profiled on RTX 3070 Ti)
body: While investigating potential instruction-level optimizations for the AWQ CUDA GEMM kernel (`gemm_forward_4bit_cuda_m16nXk32` in csrc/libtorch_stable/quantization/awq/gemm_kernels.cu), I ran an Nsight Compute (`ncu`) profile to evaluate the bottlenecks. The profile reveals that the hand-written CUDA kernel is heavily memory-bound, specifically at the L1/TEX cache layer, rather than compute-bound. * **GPU:** NVIDIA RTX 3070 Ti (Ampere, Compute Capability 8.6) * **CUDA Version:** nvcc --version nvcc: NVIDIA (R) Cuda compiler driver Copyright (c) 2005-2026 NVIDIA Corporation Built on Tue_Jun_09_02:43:40_PM_PDT_2026 Cuda compilation tools, release 13.3, V13.3.73 Build cuda_13.3.r13.3/compiler.38244171_0 * **vLLM Branch:** `main` **Optimization** Premise - For $N=128$, the loop executes 8 times. You currently use 8 inline PTX instructions inside the loop (4 sub.f16x2 + 4 fma.rn.f16x2). Precomputing the scaled zero outside the loop adds 8 instructions to the preamble but removes 4 instructions from the inner loop. Total instructions saved per thread per block: $4 \text{ instructions} \times (N/16) - 8 \text{ setup instructions}$. For $N=128$, this is a net reduction of 24 PTX instructions per thread. Modified Code - Unmodified Code - **Observations** - Instruction Optimization is Ineffective: I attempted to optimize the inner loop by precomputing - (zero * scale) and replacing the sub and fma sequence with a single fma. Benchmarking showed only a ~2% latency reduction (e.g., 0.1282 ms -> 0.1254 ms for M=64, K=4096, N=4096), confirming that instruction latency is largely hidden by memory latency. - Correctness Drift: The FMA optimization also resulted in FP16 rounding drift (max_diff = 0.125) compared to the baseline (q - z) * s execution order, making it unviable for model accuracy. title: Post sampled-result receives closer to T+PP consumption
body: - In MRV2 pipeline parallelism, non-last ranks can post sampled-result receives several local feedback steps before consumption. A receiver-side NCCL kernel can remain active while independent model work runs. - Deferring PP4 receivers by three feedback steps improved output throughput by approximately 18% on a short-generation, prefill-heavy workload and by 4--6% on two decode-heavy workload classes, with all requests completing. - Moving a due delayed receive from before to after the current model execution produced another 4.8% gain on the prefill-heavy workload in a same-configuration comparison and nearly eliminated sampled-result receive/model overlap in the captured PP0 window. - The current best jointly tuned configuration combines delay 3, post-model launch, and a retuned PP partition. Relative to the earlier delay-3 configurations, it improves output throughput by approximately 5--11% across the three workload classes. Those numbers are combined tuning results, not isolated post-model effects. - Draft PR [#53948](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/53948) currently contains the deferred-receive prototype only. The post-model ordering experiment is a separate follow-up prototype and is not yet in that PR. Model Runner V2 pipeline parallelism returns sampled results from the last PP rank to every non-last rank. The CUDA implementation uses a sibling process group and side stream, as introduced by [#42187](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/42187). However, a non-last rank posts its receive in local feedback step `T`, while the result is not consumed until `T + pp_size`. If the last rank has not produced the result yet, the receiver-side NCCL broadcast kernel can remain active across several intervening model executions. A side stream removes default-stream ordering, but does not isolate GPU execution and communication resources. The pending receive can therefore slow otherwise independent model work. title: DSA indexer is computed redundantly on every TP rank (NVIDIA / CUDA)
body: On DeepSeek-V4-Flash the DSA indexer is executed in full on **every tensor-parallel rank**, so with TP=8 seven eighths of that work is duplicated. It is **15.9 % of prefill GPU time** at ISL 131072 on 8×H100. The redundancy is recoverable by sharding the **query-row** dimension — rows are independent, so only the int32 top-k indices need merging (16 MB, not the `q × N` logits tensor). I implemented this out-of-tree and measured **+7.1 % prefill at ISL 65536 and +13.8 % at 131072** (concurrency 1, intervals disjoint). title: Avoid scanning the full KV block table
body: In the V1 scheduler path, `FullAttentionManager.get_num_common_prefix_blocks()` scans the allocated KV blocks to determine the common prefix. With only a single allocated request, this scan can traverse the request's block table even though the resulting common-prefix information cannot enable cascade attention for the single-request case. This was found during a **WOB** source audit. WOB is an experimental, novel way of improving source code for data processing. WOB is based on the idea that not all computation has equal marginal value. If a cheap mechanism can identify cases where additional work is unlikely to improve the result enough to justify its cost, that work can be selectively avoided. WOB is mostly automated, directed by a human. For long-context decode, the scan is repeated and its CPU cost grows linearly with the number of allocated KV blocks. **File:** **Section:** **Method:** Current implementation: For a single allocated request: and its allocated blocks normally have: The loop can therefore continue through the request's entire common-prefix block range. The resulting `num_common_prefix_blocks` is propagated downstream for cascade-attention handling, but the FlashAttention cascade heuristic rejects cascade attention for batches with fewer than eight requests. Consequently, in the single-request case the scheduler can pay the full block-table traversal cost for information that cannot enable cascade attention. title: Best practices for preventing GPU OOM in production
body: We are using vLLM to serve large language models in a production environment. Our primary requirement is **production stability and avoiding GPU OOM**, rather than maximizing GPU utilization or throughput. We would like to ask the vLLM community and maintainers: **What are the recommended best practices for configuring vLLM to minimize or prevent GPU OOM in production?** In particular, we would appreciate guidance on: * How to choose a safe `--gpu-memory-utilization` * How to balance `--max-model-len`, `--max-num-seqs`, and `--max-num-batched-tokens` * How much GPU memory safety margin should typically be reserved * Whether `--kv-cache-memory-bytes` is recommended for production deployments * How to account for GPU memory used by CUDA Graphs, activations, NCCL, workspaces, and other runtime components * How to perform stress testing to validate that a configuration is safe before deploying it to production We understand that there may be no configuration that can mathematically guarantee zero OOM under completely unbounded workloads. Our goal is to establish a **systematic and reproducible production-sizing methodology** so that, given a fixed model, GPU configuration, `max-model-len`, and expected workload, we can determine a sufficiently safe vLLM configuration. Any recommended production deployment guidelines, sizing formulas, profiling tools, or real-world best practices would be greatly appreciated. Thank you! _No response_ _No response_

title: Improve Pixtral vision attention scaling for batched images
body: Pixtral concatenates the patch sequences for all images in an encoder batch, while attention remains semantically independent per image. On the default installation, where xFormers is unavailable, the model constructs a dense block-diagonal mask and applies SDPA to the combined sequence. The resulting attention work and mask storage scale poorly as more images are batched. This issue proposes routing both Pixtral vision implementations through vLLM's `MMEncoderAttention`, using cumulative sequence lengths to preserve per-image boundaries. This would: - use vLLM's existing multimodal attention backend selection, including FlashAttention, FlashInfer, Torch SDPA, Triton attention, and ROCm AITER; - avoid materializing the dense combined-sequence mask; - remove Pixtral's model-specific optional xFormers path; and - preserve checkpoint compatibility, preprocessing, output ordering, and token counts. Backend-specific packed metadata still needs to be respected. In particular, FlashInfer uses padded sequence-length metadata and transformed cumulative offsets, so the implementation delegates metadata construction to `MMEncoderAttention` rather than assuming the FlashAttention layout. Controlled local benchmark on an NVIDIA DGX Spark (GB10), using BF16, the 24-layer Pixtral HF vision encoder, 840 x 840 images, three warmup iterations, and ten measured iterations. title: Fused bf16→fp32 router GEMM falls back to a standalone copy kernel on ROCm
body: The MoE router gate `GateLinear` is constructed with `out_dtype=torch.float32` (`grouped_topk` requires fp32 logits). The fused fp32-output GEMM tiers in `gate_linear.py` that fold the fp32 cast into the GEMM's BLAS epilogue are all gated on `current_platform.is_cuda()`. On ROCm the gate therefore falls through to the final tier — `F.linear` in bf16 followed by a separate `output.to(fp32)` — which emits a standalone bf16→fp32 elementwise copy kernel on every MoE layer, every step. The relevant tier does `torch.mm(x, w.T, out_dtype=fp32)`, folding the fp32 cast into the GEMM epilogue. Its eligibility (`allow_cublas_router_gemm`) requires `allow_specialized_router_gemm`, which is CUDA + SM90/SM100 only. hipBLASLt supports the same `out_dtype` epilogue, so the CUDA-only gate is unnecessarily strict. In a kernel trace this shows up as a standalone running between the router GEMM and `grouped_topk`, once per MoE layer per step. Add ROCm (bias-free, bf16 weight, fp32 out) as an alternative enabling condition for `allow_cublas_router_gemm`, in both `__init__` and `set_out_dtype` (out_dtype can be set late, so both sites must agree). CUDA behavior is unchanged — the added disjunct is `current_platform.is_rocm() and ...`, which is `False` on CUDA. The fused tier then fires on ROCm and the fp32 logits come straight out of the GEMM. Verified on gfx942: `torch.mm(bf16, bf16.T, out_dtype=fp32)` matches an fp32 reference to ~6e-5. Router gate only. It does not touch the expert GEMMs or any other bf16→fp32 intermediate in the graph (genuine fp32 intermediates in the attention-residual path are left alone). - Platform: ROCm / hipBLASLt (validated on gfx942) - File: `vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/router/gate_linear.py` _No response_ _No response_

title: On RDNA, hybrid-Mamba models fall back to Triton paged attention and decode collapses at long context
body: _No response_ *Update 2026-08-28. The cause is identified and the fix exists upstream as #45916's split-KV decode kernel, which now admits gfx11 as it stands: the `on_gfx12x()` gate this report asked to widen was widened inside the PR itself on 2026-08-10, so nothing local is needed any more. Verified on gfx1100 here on both 0.23.1 and 0.27, and independently on gfx1151 and gfx1201; details under "Verified: PR #45916 fixes this on gfx1100" and "Re-measured on 0.27 as a controlled A/B" below. Everything else in this report is stock vLLM, which is still what ships.* On gfx1100, `Qwen3.6-27B` decode time per token grows from 82.5 ms at 518 tokens of context to 235.3 ms at 32K, which is 12.1 → 4.2 tok/s. A kernel-level profile puts effectively all of that growth in one place: `kernel_paged_attention_2d`, the Triton fallback used by the model's 16 full-attention layers. The 48 gated-delta-net layers are not involved. Their decode kernels cost the same at 1K and at 32K context, which is what the architecture promises and what the implementation delivers. The reason those 16 layers take the Triton path is `use_rocm_custom_paged_attention` in `vllm/platforms/rocm.py`. Its RDNA branch requires `head_size == 128` and `block_size == 16`. A FP8 prefill slower than BF16 looks like a kernel issue, and I'd like to know if this is expected, if some additional configurations are needed as a workaround, or if I should not use ModelOpt to quantize the model at all. Env: B200 sm_100, CUDA 13.0, vLLM 0.25.1, FlashInfer 0.6.13 (arch list includes sm_100). Checkpoint: modelopt 0.46, per-tensor static FP8 (FP8_DEFAULT_CFG). Served with --quantization modelopt. **Bench (`vllm bench serve`, random 300in / 64out, `--max-concurrency 64`, 1000 prompts):** | Config | req/s | TTFT P50 (ms) | TTFT P99 (ms) | TPOT P50 (ms) | TPOT P99 (ms) | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | BF16 weights | 44.4 | 547 | 922 | 13.7 | 20.2 | | FP8 weights + FP8 KV | 36.2 | 1010 | 1903 | 7.1 | 27.3 | | FP8 weights + BF16 KV | 38.8 | 660 | 2578 | 7.7 | 28.2 | | NVFP4 weights | 84.1 | 313 | 502 | 6.8 | 10.0 | Turning the FP8 KV cache off (BF16 KV) improves TTFT but leaves performance far below BF16/NVFP4, so the bottleneck is the FP8 weight GEMM at prefill, not the KV cache. **Kernel selection (`VLLM_LOGGING_LEVEL=DEBUG` serve log):** Data do not include warmup: benched after CUDA-graph capture; the FlashInfer JIT `.so` cache is static under load (no on-demand recompile at 300 or 2048 tokens), so this is steady-state kernel speed, not compilation. **Questions:** 1. title: Adopt PTX 9.4 `ldmatrix.s8.s4` (hardware INT4→INT8 expanding load) in W4A8-INT8 paths
body: PTX ISA 9.4 (CUDA 13.4.0 Developer Preview) exposes a new `ldmatrix` variant that performs **in-flight sign extension of packed INT4 to INT8 during the shared-memory matrix load**: Source data is densely packed signed 4-bit elements; the hardware expands them to signed 8-bit values in the destination fragment. This can eliminate the register-level INT4→INT8 unpack sequences (`lop3`/`prmt` bit tricks and PRMT LUTs) in our W4A8-INT8 kernels, and potentially the dequant-oriented weight interleaving in repack. Doc: PTX ISA 9.4, §9.7.16.5.15 (`ldmatrix`), https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/developer-preview/13.4/parallel-thread-execution/index.html Verified with `ptxas`/`nvdisasm` from CUDA 13.4.0 preview (`V13.4.46`), no GPU required: - `ptxas` accepts the instruction for **sm_90a, sm_100a/f, sm_103a, sm_107a/f, sm_110f, sm_120f, sm_121a** (PTX targets per doc: `sm_90a, sm_100f, sm_110f, sm_120f`). - SASS is a **single LDSM instruction** on every architecture — no unpack sequence is generated. The encoding is bit-identical across all seven targets (opcode `0x783b` = LDSM, modifier `0x9000/0x9100/0x9200` for x1/x2/x4; cf. `LDSM.16.M88` = `0x0000`, `LDSM.U4x16P64TO8.M816` = `0xa800`, `LDSM.U6x16P32TO8.M816` = `0xb000`). - Notably **Hopper (sm_90a) is supported** — the datapath appears to have existed in silicon since GH100; PTX 9.4 merely exposes it. Existing H100/H200 fleets benefit immediately. - `nvdisasm` 13.4 does not yet print a mnemonic for this modifier (hex only); expect this to be fixed in the GA release. (vLLM @ `76bf55240`, 2026-07-23) - `csrc/libtorch_stable/quantization/marlin/dequant.h:494` — `dequant<int32_t, kU4B8>`: unpacks two nibbles per pass with `(q & 0x0F0F0F0F | 0x80808080) - 0x08080808) ^ 0x80808080`, i.e. u4-with-bias-8 → s8. - `csrc/libtorch_stable/quantization/marlin/marlin_template.h:945` — `frag_b_quant` is loaded from shared memory with plain 128-bit loads over Marlin's dequant-interleaved layout, then dequanted at `marlin_template.h:1163` (`dequa

title: ~17-20% decode throughput regression from CUDA graph memory reservation (#47366 / commit 88e5e2c57)
body: _No response_ Commit `88e5e2c57be8ce6e25510c1249352a23b8a85ec4` ("[CI/Build][AMD] Fix ROCm OOM in eagle_correctness_heavy by reserving CUDA graph memory", #47366) causes a ~17-20% decode performance regression on ROCm. The change flips the CUDA-graph memory-reservation guard in `vllm/v1/worker/gpu_worker.py` from `current_platform.is_cuda()` to `current_platform.is_cuda_alike()`, which enables the reservation path on ROCm. Reverting that single line restores full performance. - GPU: AMD MI350-class, `gfx950`, TP=4 - vLLM: `v0.23.1rc1.dev998+g88e5e2c57` (editable build) - torch: `2.11.0` - Model: `amd/GLM-5.2-MXFP4` (MoE, MXFP4), `--kv-cache-dtype fp8` In `vllm/v1/worker/gpu_worker.py`, the guard around `profile_cudagraph_memory()` was changed so ROCm now reserves CUDA-graph memory. On ROCm this reduces the memory available for KV cache and measurably slows decode. Server: Client (single-stream latency, batch 1, 1024 in / 1024 out): | Build | Output throughput (tok/s) | Mean TPOT (ms) | Available KV cache | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Suspect (`is_cuda_alike`) | 69.55 / 69.65 / 69.68 | 14.25 | 158.21 GiB | | Reverted (`is_cuda`) | 83.51 / 83.54 / 83.55 | 11.86 | 166.75 GiB | | Delta | -16.7% | +20.1% | -8.54 GiB | Run-to-run variance is ~0.1% within each build, so the ~17% gap is far above the noise floor. The reservation shrinks the KV cache by ~8.5 GiB (166.75 -> 158.21 GiB) on this config. Aggregating GPU kernel time from the torch profiler trace (rank 0) shows total kernel time rising 19.5% (62.10 s -> 74.20 s), which matches the wall-clock throughput gap almost exactly. The cost is concentrated in the tensor-parallel all-reduce (`aiter allreduce_fusion_kernel_1stage`, +60%) plus a broad rise across the MoE and attention kernels. The trace was validated for dropped events via runtime/kernel correlation matching: only 0.023% of launches were unmatched (identical on both sides), so the aggregation is trustworthy. _No response_

title: The default MXFP4 quant backend of FlashInfer has slow performance, add options for backend "cute-dsl".
body: When benchmarking Qwen3-8B-like GEMM shapes with FlashInfer, I observed that MXFP4 GEMM itself provides consistent speedup over BF16, and is significantly faster than MXFP8. However, once activation quantization time is included, the default quantization backend ("cuda") causes MXFP4 performance to drop sharply. In most shapes, MXFP4 even becomes much slower than MXFP8. Switching the activation quantization backend from `"cuda"` to `"cute-dsl"` largely fixes this issue: although activation quantization still introduces overhead, MXFP4 again becomes clearly faster than MXFP8 and often remains faster than BF16. This suggests that the `"cuda"` backend of MXFP4 quantization kernel is likely the main bottleneck. (Related issue: https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/issues/2496) vLLM currently (v0.25) uses the `"cuda"` backend as the default backend for MXFP4 quantization when using FlashInfer and does not provide an option to use `"cute-dsl"`. The following benchmark uses FlashInfer's mxfp gemm kernels and quantization kernels, including: * `mm_fp4` and `mm_mxfp8` * `mxfp4_quantize` and `mxfp8_quantize` The benchmark covers four Qwen3-8B GEMM shapes: - `K=4096, N=24576` — `mlp.gateup_proj` - `K=12288, N=4096` — `mlp.down_proj` - `K=4096, N=6144` — `self_attn.qkv_proj` - `K=4096, N=4096` — `self_attn.o_proj` For each shape, multiple batch sizes were tested. Results were compared across three modes: 1. `no-quant-a`: GEMM time only, excluding activation quantization overhead 2. `cuda-backend`: GEMM + activation quantization using CUDA backend 3. `cute-dsl-backend`: GEMM + activation quantization using cute-dsl backend Formats compared: - BF16 - MXFP8 - MXFP4 All benchmarks were done independently on NVIDIA B200 GPU. When activation quantization overhead is excluded, MXFP4 is faster than BF16 in almost all cases. This indicates that the MXFP4 GEMM path itself is efficient.

title: Triton attention drops long-context decode from 3D split-KV to 2D at batch ≥ ~12, ~doubling ITL
body: The Triton unified-attention backend picks between a **2D** kernel and a **3D split-KV (flash-decoding)** kernel using a batch-size-only threshold: At runtime the 3D path is used only while `num_seqs <= seq_threshold_3D` (`vllm/v1/attention/ops/triton_unified_attention.py`), i.e. the choice is driven purely by how many sequences are needed to fill a fixed 128-CTA launch grid. It **ignores KV length**. For long-context decode this is the wrong signal. The 2D kernel reduces the entire KV serially per CTA, so once the batch grows past the (small) threshold — ~8–12 sequences on models with few KV heads — decode falls off the 3D path and inter-token latency roughly **doubles**. There is a hard ITL cliff at batch ≥ ~12. - The threshold is a function of `num_kv_heads` and a hardcoded `128`, so it does not scale with the actual device (a B200 has 148 SMs; the 2D grid is underfilled at these batch sizes) and does not react to context length at all. - The 2D path's serial per-CTA KV reduction dominates wall-clock exactly when KV is long, which is the case the current heuristic is blind to. - Model: `nvidia/Gemma-4-31B-IT-NVFP4` - Hardware: B200 ×1 (TP=1) - Workload: RAG/chat — ISL ~8000 (2400 request + 5600 shared system prompt) / OSL 1000 - Backend: Triton attention (FlashInfer falls back to Triton for head_dim 512) Sweep concurrency and observe ITL: it stays flat up to the threshold, then jumps as decode switches to the 2D kernel. | | operating cc | tok/s/gpu | tok/s/user | ITL | |---|---|---|---|---| | current | 8 | 505 | 69.8 | 14.3 ms | | desired | 19 | 848 | 51.2 | 19.6 ms | nsys on the current build shows `kernel_unified_attention` at **51.7%** of GPU kernel time (the bf16 head_dim-512 full-attention layers dominate). title: Logprob divergence between vLLM and transformers on a fine-tuned Qwen3.5-VL mobile-use model
body: I am not proposing a performance optimization or a new performance-improvement design in this issue. This report is about an observed accuracy / logprob discrepancy between vLLM and HuggingFace transformers when serving a fine-tuned Qwen3.5-VL mobile-use model. The goal is to share the observation and ask whether this type of divergence is known or expected for Qwen3.5-VL in vLLM. N/A. I observed a consistent performance gap when evaluating a fine-tuned Qwen3.5-VL model with HuggingFace transformers and vLLM. The model was fine-tuned on my own private data, so exact reproduction may be difficult. However, the usage pattern is based on Qwen’s public `mobile_use` agent example: the model emits tool calls such as `click`, `swipe`, and `terminate` in the following style: In several cases, transformers and vLLM produced almost identical logprobs for the initial structured tool-call prefix, but diverged sharply at the first action token after `"action":"`. The difference was sometimes large enough to flip the greedy argmax and change the emitted action. I understand that vLLM does not guarantee bitwise parity or exact reproducibility with transformers. I am sharing this because the divergence appears concentrated at a task-critical action-token decision point rather than being uniformly distributed across the generated sequence. For comparison, I ran similar evaluations with a fine-tuned Gemma model. With Gemma, the results across transformers and the serving engine were within a range that I would consider acceptable given normal environment and engine differences. This held for both bf16 and 4-bit quantized variants. The observed difference was less than about 0.8 percentage points. In contrast, with Qwen3.5-VL, the performance gap appeared specifically when running the model with vLLM. The issue was present regardless of whether the model was bf16 or 4-bit quantized. The observed gap was roughly 3 percentage points, which is substantially larger than what I observed wi

title: NVIDIA-Normalized-GPT (nGPT)
body: We are planning to release a model based on a new architecture called normalized transformer (nGPT) and would like to have vllm support for it. We have started the integration process of nGPT into transformers library via [this PR](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/pull/38276). Normalized Transformer (nGPT) is a novel architecture with representation learning on the hypersphere. In nGPT, all vectors forming the embeddings, MLP, attention matrices and hidden states are unit norm normalized. The input stream of tokens travels on the surface of a hypersphere, with each layer contributing a displacement towards the target output predictions. These displacements are defined by the MLP and attention blocks, whose vector components also reside on the same hypersphere. Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.01131 _No response_ _No response_

title: VLLM_CPU_KVCACHE_SPACE: docs don't match code - no 4GB default anywhere, and values are GiB
body: *In Docs* - docs/getting_started/installation/cpu.md - the "How to decide VLLM_CPU_KVCACHE_SPACE?" section says: "This value is **4GB** by default" - In the Same page, the environment variable description says: "VLLM_CPU_KVCACHE_SPACE: specify the KV Cache size (e.g, VLLM_CPU_KVCACHE_SPACE=40 means **40 GiB** space for KV cache), Default value is 0." - docs/configuration/conserving_memory.md says the default is 4 GiB. So the same page says 0 and 4GB, and the unit keeps switching between GB and GiB. *In Code* - vllm/envs.py:52 - VLLM_CPU_KVCACHE_SPACE: int | None = 0 - vllm/platforms/cpu.py:307 - the variable is only read when it's actually set, and the value is multiplied by GiB_bytes. Also marked as a legacy setting in the comment. So: - there is no 4GB default. If the variable isn't set, nothing gets overridden at all. - the value is in GiB, not GB. *Suggested fix* - remove the "4GB by default" lines and make all three places match the code (default 0, unit GiB) - since the code calls this a legacy setting, point users to --kv-cache-memory-bytes instead Happy to send a PR with these changes.

title: vLLM's default NIXL connector is ~100× slower than the push connector on non-RDMA hardware, and the fix is undocumented
body: [cuda_ipc_probe.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/31139915/cuda_ipc_probe.py) [nixl_bench.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/31139914/nixl_bench.py) [nixl-bench-pods.yaml](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/31139913/nixl-bench-pods.yaml) On hardware without RDMA, where prefill and decode share a node, vLLM's `NixlConnector` transfers KV cache at **0.5 GB/s**. Switching a single config value to `NixlPushConnector` gives **49 GB/s** on the same hardware, same pods, same NIXL and UCX build — a **~100× difference** that matches raw CUDA peer-copy bandwidth. Cause: **NIXL/UCX `cuda_ipc` serves remote PUT at full speed but falls back to TCP for remote GET.** vLLM's `pull_worker.py` issues `make_prepped_xfer("READ", ...)`, and `NixlConnector` is a backward-compatible **alias for `NixlPullConnector`**, so the familiar connector name silently selects the slow direction. This is defensible design for the hardware NIXL targets: on InfiniBand or RoCE, RDMA READ and RDMA WRITE are symmetric at line rate, so a pull-based connector costs nothing and arguably reads better, since the consumer controls when it fetches. The asymmetry only appears on `cuda_ipc`, which is only reachable for same-node transfers without RDMA. Anyone deploying on an RDMA fabric would never see this. The problem is discoverability. `NixlPushConnector` does not appear in vLLM's NixlConnector documentation, and a web search for the name returns no results. A user on commodity GPU nodes therefore hits a 100× regression with no indication that a supported fix exists. --- | item | value | |---|---| | Host | Google Cloud `g4-standard-96` (also reproduced on `g4-standard-384`) | | GPUs | 2 × NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition (SM120), 96 GB | | Interconnect | **PCIe P2P, no NVLink, no RDMA.** `nvidia-smi topo -m` = `PIX`, `can_device_access_peer(0,1) = True` | | Driver | 580 | | Image | `docker.io/vllm/vllm-openai:v0.27.1` | | NIXL | vendored 1.3.1/1.3.2; **also reproduced w

title: Add feature documentation for undocumented vLLM-specific SamplingParams fields
body: Four vLLM-specific SamplingParams fields are exposed in both the Chat Completions and Completions API protocols but have no dedicated documentation page: - `bad_words` (list[str]) — prevents specific words/phrases from being generated - `allowed_token_ids` (list[int]) — restricts generation to a whitelist of token IDs - `logprob_token_ids` (list[int]) — efficiently returns logprobs for a specific set of token IDs without fetching the full vocabulary - `repetition_detection` (RepetitionDetectionParams) — detects and terminates repetitive N-gram output early These fields have docstrings in `vllm/sampling_params.py` and are accepted by the API (via `extra_body`), but users browsing docs.vllm.ai have no way to discover them or see usage examples. **Evidence:** - `vllm/sampling_params.py` lines 278–358: field definitions with docstrings - `vllm/entrypoints/openai/chat_completion/protocol.py` and `completion/protocol.py`: both protocols expose all four fields Reference: `thinking_token_budget` received the same treatment and is now documented in `docs/features/reasoning_outputs.md`. Add docs/features/output_token_control.md covering all four parameters with: - Offline Python API examples (SamplingParams) - Online OpenAI-compatible API examples (extra_body) - Parameter reference table for RepetitionDetectionParams ✅ Checkbox: check "I have searched the existing issues and this is not a duplicate."

title: Update Quickstart documentation with Apple Silicon / Metal execution requirements and compatibility note
body: The current [Quickstart documentation](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/getting_started/quickstart/) uses `facebook/opt-125m` in its introductory Python example code (`llm = LLM(model="facebook/opt-125m")`). When following this guide on Apple Silicon devices (macOS with Metal backend enabled via `vllm-metal`), the initialization fails with `FileNotFoundError: No safetensors found in ...`. 1. **Model Weight Compatibility:** The default example model (`facebook/opt-125m`) only hosts legacy PyTorch `.bin` checkpoint files in its primary HF repository branch. However, `vllm-metal` delegates model execution on macOS to `mlx_lm`, which strictly requires model weights to be in the `.safetensors` format. Adding a small platform-specific note or selecting a `.safetensors`-native default model for the quickstart example will greatly improve the developer onboarding experience on macOS. Update the snippet in the Quickstart guide to use a small model that includes native `.safetensors` support across CUDA, ROCm, and Metal architectures alike (e.g., `Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B` or `TinyLlama/TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat-v1.0`). **Current Quickstart line:** **Proposed Quickstart line:** Add a note callout block under the Offline Batched Inference section: > **Note for Apple Silicon (Metal) Users:** > > The vllm-metal backend utilizes mlx_lm, which requires model weights formatted as `.safetensors`. If you encounter a FileNotFoundError regarding safetensors when loading models like `facebook/opt-125m`, switch to a model repository containing safetensors (e.g., `Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B`).

title: batch_invariance.md said "compute capability 9.0+" in v0.20.0–v0.22.0 while code already supported 8.0+ (fixed in v0.23.0)
body: v0.20.0-v0.22.0: The batch invariance documentation stated "compute capability 9.0 or higher" (Hopper/Blackwell), but the code actually supported Ampere (8.0+) as well. This mismatch could confuse users with Ampere GPUs (e.g., A100, RTX 30xx). title: INT8 weight-only quantization causes 4x throughput regression at batch=1 on memory-bandwidth-bound GPUs
body: The quantization page at https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/features/quantization/ lists bitsandbytes INT8 as a supported format without noting a critical batch-size dependency that causes catastrophic throughput regression in production latency-sensitive endpoints. Using Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct with bitsandbytes INT8 quantization (load_in_8bit=True, threshold=6.0) at batch=1, I measured 22,288ms mean latency versus 5,275ms for FP32 a 4.2x slowdown. This is counterintuitive because INT8 reduces memory footprint from 12.4GB to 3.4GB, yet throughput degrades by 4x at small batch sizes. Root cause: bitsandbytes emits the warning MatMul8bitLt: inputs will be cast from torch.bfloat16 to float16 at each layer. The dequantization pass adds a separate memory movement step before each matmul. On a memory-bandwidth-bound workload like single-request serving, this overhead dominates entirely. PyTorch CUDA profiling confirmed linear and matmul operations consume 34% of total CUDA execution time while attention consumes only 0.2%, so any extra memory movement in the linear path is expensive. At batch=16 the regression disappears. The problem is specifically small batch sizes, which are exactly the conditions in latency-sensitive production endpoints. Hardware: NVIDIA L4, 23.7GB VRAM, 121 TFLOPS FP16, CUDA 12.8, PyTorch 2.10.0, vLLM 0.18.0, bitsandbytes 0.43.0. Reproduction script: from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, BitsAndBytesConfig import torch, time quant_config = BitsAndBytesConfig(load_in_8bit=True) model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( "Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct", quantization_config=quant_config, device_map="auto" ) tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct") prompt = "Explain the difference between supervised and unsupervised learning." inputs = tokenizer(prompt, return_tensors="pt").to("cuda") for _ in range(5): with torch.no_grad(): model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=100, do_sample=False) torch.cuda.synchronize()

title: cu129 Nightly Installation Resolves to CUDA 13 Wheel
body: The latest wheel available on the cu129 nightly channel is `0.20.2rc1.dev233+g5497ffbf7.cu129`, while PyPI now publishes `0.20.2` as the final release (built against CUDA 13). Per PEP 440, the cu129 pre-release version sorts below the PyPI stable release, causing the documented installation command to resolve to the PyPI artifact: This command installs `vllm 0.20.2`. Every compiled `.so` in the resulting installation links against `libcudart.so.13` (confirmed via `readelf -d`), causing CUDA 12 environments to fail at import with `ImportError: libcudart.so.13`. Under a healthy release flow, cu129 nightlies should be versioned ahead of the stable release (for example, `0.20.3rc1.devN+cu129`) and would win resolution, allowing the documented command to behave as intended. The artifact catalog at `wheels.vllm.ai/nightly/cu129/` appears to be stalled.
label: documentation
